speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear to hon. members what the situation is with respect to this measure. I wish to observe at the outset that we have now come almost to the middle of this specially called session of parliament, and today for the first time we are faced with *an urgent measure. We may ask ourselves why it is urgent. It is urgent for the simple reason, and no other, that this session was called in December rather than in January.
Before taking my seat I hope I shall have shown the house that this is the only urgent measure the government has brought before us. AH their other plans were conceived and put dnto effect before we came here, and we are asked now to act only as rubber stamps, to approve something that has been done.
What is this measure before us? It is an address to His Excellency the Governor General from the House of Commons asking that the Transitional Measures Act, 1947, be extended from December 31, 1947, to March 31, 1948. What is the Transitional Measures Act, 1947? It is a temporary act conferring very wide powers on the government to control the Canadian economy. When that act was passed, as the minister has said, it was the intention *that it should continue until March 31, or until two months after parliament met, if it met next year. But there is a provision in the act that if parliament met in November or December, 1947, the act would terminate on December 31, 1947. So it is clear that if parliament had met in October, or if it had not opened until January next, this measure would not have been required at all. It has been made necessary now by the fact that we have been called together in December instead of January or February next. It is clear that the resolution before us would never have been necessary if we had met in October, or if we had met at the usual time after the New Year.
We are now asked by this address to cure the situation the government has created by coming here at this time. If we pass this resolution, the condition which was created last May when the act was passed, and which has been undone by the government's calling us here now, would be restored. That is what the minister has said, and that is our understanding.

For a few moments I wish to review the situation in which we find ourselves. The government told us we were being called here to deal with a crisis. Now that we are here we find that the government has already acted, that it has already taken steps to cure the crisis, and that those steps are now in effect. As I have said, we are called here just to approve measures which are already in effect, to approve what has already been done. It is true that what the government has done will have to be approved by legislation, but it was not necessary that that legislation be passed in December. It would have been just as effective if it had been passed in January or February. What then is the reason for our being here in December? The reason for our being here is that the government may spread itself in connection with these Geneva trade agreements and thus distract the attention of the public from the other more objectionable measures that are to be brought forward later.
What are the measures that the government tells us it was important should be dealt with in December; what are the measures that they speak of as being necessary to cure this crisis?
First, they said there are these trade agreements. Then there are the taxation measures. And there are the special emergency measures for the restriction of imports, what I choose to call the totalitarian powers act.
Let us look at these measures and see whether action by parliament at this particular time is necessary.
Let us take the trade agreements first. We have discussed them for some time, but they have been left unfinished. The government says that it does not intend to proceed with them any further at this time. That was clear from the beginning. In the Prime Minister's first address to this house he indicated that they would be brought forward and discussed for a couple of days and then left over to be dealt with later on, because it would take weeks to deal with them. It was quite clear that the government did not intend that they should be finally dealt with at this early part of the session. It is very clear then that they are not an urgent matter to be dealt with at this session. But even if they had been an urgent matter, they could have been dealt with as other agreements of this kind have been dealt with in the past, by order in council under the Customs Act. The law is there providing for that action. That course was followed in the past by the government but it was not followed in this instance. As I said yesterday, they have been brought forward now merely as window-dressing for what is to follow.

Transitional Measures Act
Then we have the excise tax and other measures. These taxes have already been imposed and are now being /collected. In this connection let me refer to the statement made over the air on November 17 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who said:
At the coming session of parliament a special bill will be introduced concerning these emergency restrictions. In order to avoid widespread anticipation and evasion of these restrictions in the next few weeks, which would cost us many millions of dollars that we cannot afford,

The minister recognized the fact that delay had cost and would cost us many millions of dollars. He continued:

we will ask parliament to make this new law apply as from midnight tonight, and we will put these restrictions into effect in advance, as we do in the case of budget proposals.
As lion, members know, when the budget is brought down the minister tells us that it contains certain financial provisions which will go into effect that night, but they are not then legally in effect. It is simply a warning to all who may be affected that they will be brought into effect and apply as of the date stated. Then later on they are brought into effect by legislation. That could have been done in this matter just as well in January or February as in December. The minister went on:
This can be done under the provisions of the Foreign Exchange -Control Act. At the time this act was passed the government did not believe that such power was contained in the act but we are now advised by the law officers of the crown that it provides the legal basis for such restrictions as are proposed.
As I said, these measures are in effect. The government brought them into effect, and we say that they brought them into effect illegally and unconstitutionally. But whether or not that is the case, the fact is that they are in effect and they are being carried out. We did not need to meet in December rather than January in order to make them effective. That is the point I am making in connection with these taxation measures and the other measures announced as being urgent.
The proposed emergency measures are already in effect under the Foreign Exchange Control Act. Imports are being restricted by embargoes and quotas. We take the position that for the moment those are phony powers, they are usurped powers. What we are asked to do now is to provide some basis of legality ; that is all. They have been put into effect by a measure which the government itself and the government experts said would never be used for that purpose. However, finding themselves in the situation where they needed to
take action, they used it and now we are asked to provide some respectable legal basis for what has been done.
It is clear, therefore, that these three measures are in effect and that we did not need to be called here in December to do anything more about them. Everything could have been done just as well in January. It may be said that we asked for an early session to deal with the nation's crisis. So we did. We asked for a session to discuss these problems in order to arrive at what should be done. But we now find that the government has taken its own action and all we are asked to do is to approve what has been done and is in effect.
So, as I have said, we come now to the only emergent measure that is before the house, the continuation of the Transitional Measures Act, 1947. This act is to be extended for three months. The Agricultural Products Act is in the same position. As I say, those are (he only measures before us that are urgent. And they have been made urgent by calling us here in December rather than January. This seems to be a session where the government starts everything and finishes nothing, and creates the only urgent problem-
Some lion. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
There is no question but that we are sitting here in December and that the session was called now rather than later on for the purposes of the government and nothing else. What I said was that this was a specially called session, and so it was, and so it was represented by the government itself. Nobody in Canada misunderstands that. And now we are being asked to remedy a situation that results from the government's own
Transitional Measures Act

(mismanagement in this respect. That is what rit amounts to.
What are the facts as to the crisis-the real (crisis, not this temporary crisis? The first is that the government did not perceive the crisis early enough, and when it did perceive ;it, it acted too late; and when it did act it acted improperly and in an ill-conceived manner. Nevertheless its plans are now in [DOT]effect and we are called into session only to [DOT]approve of them. This resolution then is the only urgent problem with which the government has to deal.
Why did the government call us into special session? Only the Almighty and the Prime Minister know, but I think the Canadian people understand that we were called here just in order that they might be confused.
As to the measure itself, we have no time to deal with it adequately. If we did, it would take all the time of this specially called session. The government will pass this measure anyway. It was the law until March 31 next ibut for the government's mismanagement. No doubt there are some things in the measure which will need to be preserved so long as the government's policies result in the severe shortages we have today, but only *under those conditions and no others.
Bringing this measure before us now raises two questions. It raises the question of the principle of controls, the principle of the government's undertaking to run the nation's economy. It raises also the question of the success of the government in administering the controls which it has already had. I wish to touch briefly on these two questions.
In wartime the government asked for wide powers and the nation freely granted them- powers to control prices, powers to control wages, powers to allocate workers to jobs, powers to impose rigid price ceilings, powers to control costs, powers to control profits. Under those conditions a good job was done during the war. But if you remove any one of those controls you create conditions under which you will not get those results. When peacetime came the government came along and said: We want a continuation of those powers. And the government then took some and left out others. But its efforts to control our economy have failed. As I said, unless we have all these controls right through from one end to the other, they must necessarily fail. And to have them all means going to the extreme regimentation and takes us clear into the field of communism and totalitarianism.
We take the position that the government having undertaken to control the economy and

having failed, it is now answerable to the public. The fundamental position is this, that the government has both expanded credit and restricted supplies by controls so that now there is a greater supply of credit than of goods, with the inevitable result of rising prices. And now the government is attempting by the partial use of controls to correct that situation.
Our position is that when you apply one control to correct one condition you raise two problems elsewhere, and when you use controls again to correct those two problems, you have four problems on your hands. We do not believe in the principle of restrictive controls except under very emergent conditions.
Some people have distinguished between controls and subsidies. The government itself has done that. The minister who introduced this bill has done it. In discussing his revaluation plans, as reported in Hansard of July 5, 1946, at page 3181, he had occasion to comment on subsidies, and he said this:
The fourth matter which I wish to mention is that the policy of paying subsidies will remain in effect in order to prevent undue increases in prices of articles of major importance in the consumer's cost of living or in primary producer's costs of production.
That was the position the minister took with respect to subsidies on July 5 of last year.
Now I want to touch on the way in which the government has used the powers given to it under its emergency legislation. I shall give two or three illustrations. First of all, take milk. That was dealt with in this house more than a year ago. and - the majority of this house took the position that the subsidy-should not be removed. But after the house adjourned, the government, following out its own policies, did remove the subsidy and the price of milk went up.
I might also mention what was done in connection with flour, or wheat, or bread. The subsidy for wheat was taken off, the subsidy which the government gave to millers who bought wheat to be made into flour to be consumed as bread in Canada. That subsidy was removed and the price of wheat to millers went up, the price of flour followed, and the price of bread followed that. I just want to point out that while the government had that power, it chose to exercise it at the very worst possible time it could have chosen. Here we have an export commodity, wheat. We sell three times as much of it as we consume in Canada, or nearly so. The price of wheat is dependent upon outside conditions and fluctuates widely. It may be 40 cents or it may be $3.40 a bushel; we have seen as

Transitional Measures Act
wide a fluctuation as that in the past fifteen years. But this parliament in its wisdom has said that to prevent prices getting so low- they once reached 40 cents-we are going to establish price floors. We are not by that legislation going to let it drop like that. Even if it does drop that far outside, we are not going to let it drop that far at home. The legislation provides that we are going to subsidize the producer in order to protect him and in order to protect our economy.
You have the right, which you exercised until a few months ago, with regard to wheat for Canadian use, that when the price was high you would see that for bread it was subsidized. The subsidies which had until then been applied were taken off at a time when wheat prices had reached the highest point in our history. They have gone up a little higher since then. When prices went up the government chose to take off the bread subsidy. What could happen but that the price of bread would rise, jwith a commodity selling at 40 cents at one time and eight times 40 cents at another time? Are we going to protect the producer when the price is low and refuse to protect the consumer when it is high? My criticism is that that was the wrong time to take the subsidy off, and that taking it off then could not help but result in increasing bread prices; and those prices, added to the rising cost of living in other commodities, give rise to unrest among workers, causing threats of strikes and all that kind of thing. My criticism is that that was not the time to take off the subsidy.

speechtext: You asked for it.

speechtext:
I never did ask for it.
I am speaking now of the way in which the government has administered the powers that we gave it.
Let me now touch on another control that you misused. You were giving subsidies and you had a price ceiling on coarse grain. By your control and by your marketing policies you had frozen the prices of the finished products of the farmers. By your contracts with Britain you had frozen farm prices and made them more or less fixed. They were influenced a little by some that was sold outside but they were largely fixed. Then by removing all your controls on costs you let the cost of production go up, with the result that every branch of the livestock industry across this country is now fearful of the future. They feel that under these conditions the possibility to make a profit has gone. They say the government controls are not working out fairly.
But the worst criticism of all is that you chose to do that in the middle of the marketing season. If I remember correctly, up to October 20 these controls were on, and these subsidies were on. The prices received by those who had grain to sell were low. Then you took off these ceilings, and you took off the subsidies, and the next day the prices were 20 cents to 30 cents a bushel higher. You have made one section of the producers of Canada take low prices and have allowed others to get high prices on the same commodity. I say, Mr. Speaker, that there can be no excuse for the government taking that action at the time it did. It should have been done either at the beginning of the marketing season or at the end of it. You have created an inequity in this way, an inequity which you will find no means of correcting short of dipping into the treasury of the dominion in order to do so.
I shall speak now about the administration of another control. It has to do with the question of another cereal; I refer to rye. Rye is a cereal which is actually worth less than wheat, from the point of view of its food value. That commodity was not controlled by the government. The result was that the price went up to $4 or thereabouts a bushel, at a time when this government had sold two-thirds of the wheat crop of the Canadian farmer for $1.55 a bushel, yet here was a cereal worth less than wheat finding a world price of S4. What happened? The price of rye was not so high in the United States. The farmers there were getting about S3 a bushel for their rye. Canadians on this side went over there, bought this rye at around
53	a bushel, paid 9 cents a bushel tariff on it, brought it into Canada and then sold it at
54	a bushel, thus making nearly SI 'a bushel, just by bringing it across th" line.
The point I want to make is this. In order to buy that rye they had to get United States dollars, of which we were short in this country. They were allowed by the government's regulations to get those United States dollars in this country in order to bring in rye from another country, which rye was immediately sold outside of Canada. Our United States dollars were used for that purpose at a time when we were short of United States dollars. Somebody here is surely responsible for that.
You asked for control of our economy in wartime. The nation gladly gave you the powers you asked for. The war is over. You asked for emergency powers in peacetime, and that request too was granted, but with many misgivings. Under your administration, by the powers you have used or failed to use, you
Transitional Measures Act

have failed to solve the problems you wanted to solve, and we are in the situation we are in today, which everybody admits is not good. Under your administration, your use of these controls has failed to correct the conditions you set out to correct. As I said, your attempts to solve certain problems have created others, and you have misused certain powers you have. I do not question the integrity or even the ability of the men who are trying to control the nation's economy, Mr. Speaker, but I do say that this all goes to show that a few people here in Ottawa cannot regulate the nation's economy satisfactorily.
T-he government asked for all these powers; it got the powers it asked for. It has made its own bed; now it is asking for three months in which to lie in it. I want to say to the government that we are willing to grant that reprieve. But if you do not make a better job in the next three months than you did in the last nine, you will not be facing a complacent House of Commons when you come back here again. You will find yourselves facing the wrath of the people, particularly the farmers, the workers and the businessmen. And you will face the indignation of the members who are sent here to represent them, and you will face it not only from this side but from all sides of the house. While we are granting this reprieve for three months, I promise you a critical appraisal of your acts by this party, and I imagine by other parties as well, and certainly by the Canadian people.

speechtext:
I note from the order paper, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is to move another bill, and there is another resolution-the bill dealing with emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources, and the resolution dealing with agricultural products. Therefore I do not expect to follow the example of the leader of the opposition and discuss these two other measures today. I intend as nearly as I can to keep to the problem which is before the house in the resolution which has been moved this afternoon by the Minister of Justice.
First of all, I think that the problem before us is one of the gravest that parliament has had to face for many a long day. I am glad as a matter of fact that parliament was called at this particular time because it gives Parliament an opportunity to discuss the problem that most nearly affects the people of the country, namely, the cost of living. Because of that, apart altogether from the other measures that are to come before us, made 
necessary by various actions of the government, which we can discuss on another occasion, I am glad that we are here today with this opportunity. My only regret is that the resolution now before us does not extend the time of these emergency powers beyond March 31, because I am quite convinced that in the next three or four months the condition we now have will become aggravated on account of the other policies which the government has adopted and which the Minister of Finance announced about three weeks ago.
So I say that it is because of that condition that in my opinion the extension of powers is insufficient to meet the needs of the present situation. To those who do not believe that these powers should be extended, but that they should be discontinued as soon as possible, what are the alternatives? Well, the alternatives that are suggested by what you might call the more or less classical old-fashioned conservative economists of this country, the free-enterprisers of laissez-faire, are really three in number, and they worked very well for some people half a century ago when the world was a different sort of world and the economy under which we operated was a different sort of economy.
In those days they would have suggested immediately that in order to meet a situation such as this there should be an increase in the rates of interest. They would probably have suggested, if the condition had been as we have it now, what some of the people are suggesting today, that is, that we should devalue the dollar. Now the devaluation of the dollar in a country where we depend so largely upon imparts for many of our commodities in manufactured goods, for so many of our supplies in the way of food and other materials-things like raisins and currants from California, grapefruit, oranges and orange juice which we need in this climate, as well as vegetables from the United States, which is a source of fresh vegetables in the depth of winter, and materials such as cotton and so on-the devaluation of the dollar, I say, entering into the cost of these basic articles, would further raise the cost of living for the hard-pressed people of the country. Consequently I have always been in support of the policy which has been followed of resisting all attempts to devalue the Canadian dollar. In my opinion at least it would have benefited only a small group of people, particularly those who own and not those who work; because the workers who work in the gold mines would have found their cost of living mounting and would have suffered with all the rest of the people who work for their living, wherever they may be employed in this country.

Transitional Measures Act
The third suggestion that has been made is one that is being made also by some influential newspapers. Take for example an article which appeared some weeks ago in the London Economist that labour might be compelled to move from one industry to another in Great Britain, and in other countries as well, by creating a pool of unemployment. A pool of unemployed would tend to bring down costs, so these so-called classical economists claim. But compulsory hunger-

speechtext:
Anyone who knows anything about United Kingdom policies knows this, as I said in the debate on the address the other afternoon: An attempt has been made in that country to redistribute wealth so that those who were badly underfed might be more nearly fed, and those who were overfed have got to share the austerity with everybody else. But hon. members like the hon. member for Rosedale do not like that kind of policy.
As far as we in this country are concerned, in common with other countries, we are pledged to do certain things, pledged as members of the united nations organization. Chapter 9, setting up the economic and social council of the united nations, article 55a, commits us to the policy of higher standards of living, full employment, and conditions of economic and social progress and development. So the suggestion that is made from
time to time for the creation of a pool of unemployment is one that we could not accept if we wished to remain loyal members of the united nations organization and fulfil its obligations.
The policy now before us for the extension of these controls does to some extent amount to a reversal of the government's position of eight or ten months ago, and indeed more recently than that, when the controls were taken off in September and October. As I said the other afternoon, and I repeat it, we have stood solidly in favour of the continuance of controls as long as they were essential to the welfare of the Canadian people.
My Social Credit friend (Mr. Low) was in his seat a moment ago, and I am sorry he has left the chamber, but he said the other afternoon that I had misinterpreted his remarks regarding the position of the Social Credit, group. Well, I looked up the speech that was made by my hon. friend on March 21 of the current year and while I admit there are a number of what I regard as conflicting statements in the speech, I find this:
On the one hand, the controls-
Dealing with the wartime controls.
-may have been introduced for the purpose of restricting production of certain goods and services, especially those for home consumption,, so that the maximum effort could be diverted' into the production of materials for war. Now-that the war is over it can only be common sense, it seems to me, that the cure for the-shortage of homes is not to continue indefinitely-to control rents. The sensible cure is to embark upon an adequate program of building of dwelling houses which will ensure all Canadian families having homes of their own.
With that statement I cordially agree. I point out, however, that you cannot build enough houses for the Canadian people in the course of a few months; and in the meantime the continuance of rent control is an absolute necessity for the protection of the great masses of the Canadian people.
Similiarly. Mr. Speaker, it seems to me foolish to continue a rigid control of prices which was an emergency measure designed mainly to restrict certain kinds of production. Rather it seems to me that by removing every possible barrier to it-
Which I presume would include controls.
-production should be increased to the utmost, in order that through competition to please customers, the control of prices will be exercised by the people through the things they have to. buy.
I read into that what I think any hon. gentleman would read into it, opposition to the continuance of controls; and if I have done tho hon. gentleman an injustice I cannot help it, for that seems to be the plain interpretation of the words I have just read.

I want to say something this afternoon, however, about the statement that price controls are necessary because of the great increase in the cost of living, due in part at least to a phenomenal increase in wages. The other afternoon the Minister of Finance, in dealing with this matter, placed before the house some percentage increases. I have taken the trouble to look at these statistics of average hours of work and average weekly earnings from the beginning of 1947. I may say this has a very material bearing on the question of the extension of controls, the subject we are discussing, because I believe these controls are essential in the interests of the great majority of consumers who are wage earners, workers in agriculture, farmers, fishermen and so on throughout this country. Since this one phase was mentioned the other afternoon I just want to take a look at some of these wages, and I am referring to the report of the government's own bureau of statistics, employment statistics branch, under the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have before me the issue of November 10, 1947, and am looking at the moment at page 9, if anyone wishes to check. To be perfectly fair about it I am going to take some of the low, some of the medium, and some of the comparatively high weekly wages. Some may call them comparatively high, but let us see whether they are sufficient to maintain a reasonable standard of living.
First, let us take manufacturing. As at September 1, 1947, the average weekly rate for all manufacturing industries was S34.77. If we look at the workers engaged in animal products, edible, we find that at that date the average weekly rate was S31.95. For dairy products it was $32.08; for meat products, 833.70. Of course since then there has been a strike and the wages are up slightly, but only slightly. . The cost of boots and shoes has gone up considerably, but the average weekly rate of workers in that industry was $24.32. In lumber products it was $31.52; for rough and dressed lumber, 132.74. Then, as I said the other afternoon, the price of canned fruits and vegetables has increased in the last twelve -months by about 100 per cent, according to the newspapers. The average weekly rate in this canning industry was $22.50. In chocolate and cocoa products, which have gone up substantially, it was S23.17. Textile products also are up tremendously; there the average weekly rate was $25.60. In thread, yarn and cloth, it was $27.08; cotton yarn and cloth, $26.37; woollen yarn and cloth. $27.11; silk and artificial silk, $28.21; hosiery and knit goods, $23.34; garments and personal furnishings.

$24.07. In tobacco, which has gone up very considerably, it was $26.02; electrical apparatus, $34.94; primary iron and steel, $44.48; agricultural implements, $38.62; sheet metal work, $34.82; mining, $42.67; highway construction, which is largely common labour, $28.35; personal, including chiefly laundries, $22.82.
These are the average weekly wages, including of course all classes of weekly wages, given by the bureau of statistics. Now if we look at the cost of living we can see how these compare. It is all very w-ell to say that wages have gone up since 1939. Food prices have gone up since 1939, because both the producer of food and the man engaged in common labour or industrial labour were at that time badly under-remunerated, and consequently one would have expected the increases to be considerable on a percentage basis. But if we look at the statement of the Toronto welfare council in 1944, which incidentally is the last I can find, it was estimated that a family of five required $1,864 a year in order to meet their bare living costs.' At that time the cost of living index stood at 119. On September 1 of this year the cost of living index stood at 136-4. This means an increase of 17 per cent since 1944.
On this basis it will be seen that a family needing $1,864 in 1944 would have needed at least $2,181 as of September 1 of this year, or an average weekly wage of $41.94. Compare this with the average weekly wages I have already given as of September 1 of this year, from the official document from which I quoted. For example, the average in the manufacturing industries was $34.77 and in highway construction it was $28.35. If you look at another aspect of the government's price inflationary policies, for such they have been, it will be seen by comparing the increase in the cost of living from April 1, 1945, to September 1, 1947, with the increases in wages in that period. During that time the cost of living rose almost 18 per cent while manufacturing wages rose 13 per cent and mining wages 15 per cent. Highway construction wages rose at the same rate as the cost of living, but the weekly wage on September 1 in that particular field stood at $28.35 according to the government's own statistics.
I said I was opposed to the use of inflation as a means of rectifying our condition. I have here support for that statement in an authoritative textbook that has been in use in local universities, particularly in the economics class at Carleton college. It is called "Introduction to Monetary Theory" by Chandler. If we look at that we see the effect of inflation. He

quotes from a famous Italian economist dealing with what happened after the last war, and says:
Inflation was always a terrible instrument for the redistribution of wealth. It is not possible to study the influence of the inflation separately from those of other causes which acted at the same time, e.g., the war. But it may be said that on the whole the inflation generally favoured the entrepreneurs and the owners of the material means of production, especially strengthening the positions of industrial capitalists; that it caused a lowering of the real wrages of workmen; that it decimated or destroyed altogether the old middle class of investors, possessors of those securities which now could only, ironically, be said to show a fixed income; and that it created a new middle class of intermediaries, traders, small speculators and the bourse-
Stock exchanges, the grain exchange, in our Canadian terms.
-and small profiteei-s of the monetary depreciation.
Consequently we have stood solidly for beneficial controls. Once again, when we talk of price controls, we are talking of something within the power of this parliament itself.
I notice that the press continues to say: Why not the control of wages? I believe I have given the answer as to why wages do not need to be controlled at this particular time. But the other answer I gave, and will give again, is that the control of wages has been returned to the provinces and that it does not lie within the province of this government.
I notice, for example,' it was stated that in addressing the C.C.F. members yesterday Mr. Pat Conroy, who is seeing members of all parties in the house-I do not know whether lie is seeing them separately or collectively; but I know we suggested it would save our time if he would see us collectively, and that was done yesterday morning. I was about to say that I noticed in this morning's Gazette it reports Mr. Conroy as saying, "Prices, yes; wages, no". That is not what the secretary of the Canadian Congress of Labour said yesterday. I have before me the official release which was given the press gallery, and which I did not see until this afternoon. I should like to put it on record, in fairness to the gentlemen and the lady who sit around me, and to the gentleman who appeared before us yesterday morning, because I believe this is a true statement of what happened. It states:
The position of the Canadian Congress of Labour with respect to re-imposing control of wages was outlined today by Pat Conroy, secretary-treasurer of the congress, at a meeting of C.C.F. members of the House of Commons. Mr. Conroy was accompanied by a delegation
composed of members of C.C.L. unions who are currently interviewing members of parliament on prices.
"The suggestion has been advanced, both by the Minister of Finance and by Progressive Conservative members of the House of Commons, that a return of price control would automatically mean a return of wage controls," Mr. Conroy said.	_	,
"Organized labour recognizes that it is theoretically possible for wages to reach such a point that they would have to be checked if further price increases were to be avoided."
I do not know what that means if it does not mean that theoretically the time might come when a control of wages might have to be exercised, but that stage certainly has not yet been reached in the Canadian economy. The figures I put on record this afternoon indicate that that statement of Mr. Conroy is true. He goes on to say:
First it should be clearly understood that talk of wage control is a fed herring which some people, who are defending the increasing profits of large corporations, are trying to draw across the path of those who are seeking the restoration of prices to reasonable levels.
The dominion government, by the admission of its own finance minister lacks the power to re-impose wage controls. The government which the minister represents has deliberately returned this power to the provinces with a view to getting rid of such troublesome questions. The government has very definitely, however, the power to re-impose price controls.
Labour will certainly not agree to the freezing of wages in their present relationship to prices. In his address to the Commons yesterday, Mr. Abbott said that wages, on an index basis, had kept pace with prices since 1939. The figures which he placed on the record failed entirely to show the dollars and cents position of Canadian workers, both in 1939 and now.
I have placed on record this afternoon the supporting 1947 figures from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. Mr. Conroy goes on to say:
Largest increase reported by Mr. Abbott was in logging. The average weekly wage in that industry in 1939 was only $16.44. In manufacturing it was only $23.24. Coupled with this is the fact that figures of average earnings for salaried and wage earners combined, which Mr. Abbott used, are not a good index of wage earners. In 1939 average weekly earnings of wage earners alone in manufacturing were $20.11, which was $3.13 less than the average for wage and salary earners, combined.
There has obviously been an increase, but the money the average Canadian worker receives today in his pay envelope is far from sufficient to meet the essential requirements of his family at today's prices.
Mr. Abbott quotes the cost of living index at 143-6 to Illustrate increases in living costs. He did not mention that the food index, which is most important to Canadian workers, now stands at 173-6 and the clothing index, another vital factor is at 157.

The Canadian Congress of Labour believes that price controls should be restored and action should be taken by fully representative public bodies to establish a proper relationship between prices, wages and profits. That condition does not now exist and until it does we shall be faced with economic confusion and unbalance.
That is a summary, incidentally, of what the secretary of the Canadian Congress of Labour said to us yesterday morning, and what I imagine he will be saying to hon. members of other political groupings in the house.
I said a minute ago that since the beginning of the war the cost of living index has risen from 100-8 in August 1939. The index, of course, upon which this is based is an index of prices between 1935 and 1939. So on August 1, 1939, the index was roughly 100. At that time the food index was at the low point of 99-3-and may I say it was far too low.
In 1941 two years later, on October 1, the percentage increase since August 1, 1939 was 14-6. The total index then was 115-5, and the food index 123-2. In 1943 it had risen to 18-3 on October 1, the total index standing at 119-3 and the food index at 132-9.
In 1945-and this is the year to which I direct attention particularly-on October 1 the percentage increase was a little lower than in 1943. It stood at 18-8 as against 18-3. The total index was 119-7 and the food index was 133-3.
Then we come to 1946, a year ago. On October 1 the increase over 1939 was 25-5, with a total index of 126-8 and a food index of 146-5. But when we take the year in which the majority of controls and subsidies were removed we must bear in mind that I cannot give figures beyond November 1 of this year-and that in the last three or four weeks some very sharp increases in prices have occurred, as a result of the announcements made some three weeks ago. On October 1, 1947 the increase was 41-1, with a total index of 142-2 and a food index of 171-3. If you figure that out as of November 1, as I did, and on a percentage basis, you find that the increase over 1939 was 42-8. The total index was 143-6, the food index was 173-6, indicating very clearly the sharp increases that are now occurring month by month due to the removal of controls.
I could put many more figures on the record, but I do not intend to weary the house with them. From July up to November 1, that is for four months, there has been a rise of 7-7 points in the total index. The increase in those four months has been greater than it was in the whole twelve months of 1946. There is certainly no indication that the sharp rise

is decreasing; on the other hand all the indications are that when we get the figures for December-we shall not get them until about the time the house reconvenes-we shall find that the increase has been steeper still in the past few weeks.
May I remind the house of what the government said in January of this year. In the speech from the throne it was stated:
The policy of the government is to maintain only such price and commodity controls as maybe required to protect consumers from a sudden and drastic rise in the cost of living.
While we did not like that proviso, the government announced its policy, in that phraseology, of retaining sufficient controls-to do what? To protect the consumer from a sudden and drastic rise in the cost of living. But the government has not done that. On the contrary, what the government has dione is to permit a sudden and drastic rise in the cost of living by the removal of those controls which according to the throne speech early this year the public of Canada had a right to expect would be maintained.
Of course my hon. friends to my immediate right are in an entirely different position. They have opposed controls throughout. I have a list of the speeches they have made in the house dealing with this control business. This afternoon we heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) say that much of this was due to the manner in which controls had been removed. Obviously had the Progressive Conservative party been in power when the war ended, everything would have been thrown into the open arms of free enterprise and we would have had exactly the same price levels as they had in the United States. That would not only have affected the cost of living in our own country to a tremendous degree, it would have seriously affected the cost of commodities to those people overseas who rely on us for food and supplies.
As late as at its national meeting in Ottawa on March 31, 1946 we find a resolution adopted by the Progressive Conservative party which is reported by the Winnipeg Free Press as follows:
We are opposed in principle to continuation of every wartime wage and price ceiling and restrictive controls.
Of course that included rent control. The hon. member for Stanstead, (Mr. Hackett) for whom I have the greatest respect, has stated within the last two months, I think in the Financial Post of early October, that he believed in the policy of the removal of all controls, and he would include in that the removal of rent control. I notice the hon. gentleman nods his head in the affirmative.

It would to a totalitarian mind. I should like to make abundantly clear in just a very few minutes exactly what I did say in regard to controls last year, and more especially in regard to the two policies which I then outlined.
Let me say, to begin with, that we recognize always in emergencies such as now face us and such as have faced us for some years, that the government has to have two policies-and oftentimes, Mr. Speaker, they have more than that, some up their sleeve. But in this case I do recognize the necessity of having a long-term policy and a short-range policy. It has always been my judgment that whatever the government was doing with regard to controls was a matter of short-range policy- at least so I interpreted it. I want to make it clear now that every time this government has brought before this house a clear-cut short-range policy dealing with controls to meet emergency, this group has supported it. posal that the government has brought before us and which it justified to us. We have asked constantly and consistently that they do justify their requests. With regard to such requests we have spoken our minds freely, and while often we have taken exception to the type of control that was being proposed, we ourselves have proposed a better one which could be instituted as a long-range policy and which in time would make the bureaucratic controls unnecessary. That is the trouble with our friends to my right. They do not listen closely enough, and do not read carefully enough to get the whole picture.
Let me quote further from the same speech of mine from which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar quoted. I said:
The only effective controls are those which are inherent in a justly scientific economic structure which by its very fairness and justice induces- mind you, Mr. Speaker, I say induces-the full support of all classes of the community and will be freely sustained without compulsion of any kind. That was the position we took.
We further granted at the same time that the government required to exercise a measure of control over price structures, foreign exchange, import and export of goods, rentals, and so on; but we did urge that the government abandon bureaucratic controls as rapidly as possible-
I did not say all at once. I said as rapidly
as possible.
-and concurrently introduce a system of automatic controls that would do a better job without endangering the freedom of individuals in this country.
That is inherent in the Social Credit proposals we have placed before the house time and again. I continued:
We acknowledge the necessity of safeguarding the welfare of the people and of providing them with adequate and effective protection against evil forces that may exploit them. With us it is not a question of the need of controls; it is indeed a question of what kind of controls.
Social Crediters are implacably opposed to planned controls which enhance the power of the state at the expense of the liberties of the individuals of Canada. We vigorously oppose all such controls as vest in hordes of insolent bureaucrats authority over every phase of the lives of the people. Rather do we urge that as rapidly as possible wartime bureaucratic controls be removed, be replaced immediately by a set of effective checks and balances inherent in a revitalized and reformed financial policy, and which automatically safeguard the whole political, economic, and moral welfare of our people.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the position we take.

In the first place, Mr. Speaker, in the short-term policy to meet an emergency we are still ready to assist the government by supporting this resolution providing for an extension for a further period of three months. We do not intend at this stage to enter into a long and exhaustive discussion of whether it is needed for a longer period than three months. The time will come, when the house re-assembles after the first of the year, when that can be done. But for the present we are quite prepared to give the government another three months. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we must again insist that the whole of a long-term policy for Canada must be studied with a view to making it unnecessary to impose such controls over any lengthy period of time.
I have pointed out year after year, and I am going to point out again today, that one of the most important factors in the high cost of living is the failure of our country to produce, in the quantity needed by our people, certain of the goods and services which we can produce. While it is true that we have

had a fairly sizeable over-all production, everybody knows that the controls, restrictions, regimentation and tight-reins imposed by the government have certainly caused a reduction in the amount of production we could have had. There is not any question about that. If you go through the country talking to the people as I have during the past three months, you will soon find out what they think about these restrictions and restraints and what ft has done to the volume of Canadian production. One of the best ways in which to meet the high cost of living is to lay down a set of conditions such as will make the' people free to open for themselves the flood-gates of production of all kinds of wanted goods and services.

Sure, they voted for it. You can bet your life they did. Some of my hon. friends like tc steal the other fellow's thunder and then criticize him for suggesting it. That is their trouble.
If we are successfully to tackle this question of the high cost of living we certainly ought to start out with a mentality of abundance instead of one of scarcity such as the one my hon. friends the socialists, have; they are constantly talking in terms of scarcity and austerity and having to bring everybody down to a starvation level. We ought to be thinking Mr. Speaker, in terms of boosting and lifting everybody to an abundant level; and we can do it. That being the case, why do I not hear my hon. friends talk about some of the restrictions to that desirable high production? For example, let us take taxation. How often do we hear members of the C.C.F. group criticize, on the floor of this house, the taxation measures passed by this government and previous governments. There is not a single one of those taxation measures that they ever opposed. The simple reason for that is that their whole program depends on high taxation.

Would you not think, Mr. Speaker, with the mechanization of industry and the introduction of the use of machines that make things faster and better, that we ought to be able to get things cheaper? We would, if we did not have such an absurd financial system.
Recently, I saw a machine, with one human attendant, making shoes at the rate of 1,000 pairs a day. Surely that same type of shoe should be available to people today at less than S2, which the old shoemaker got for them in the old days. Why should we have to pay a great deal more? When one investigates one finds that the high cost is, in the main, because of the numerous taxes which - are imposed upon the manufacture of the shoes, from the time the hide is stripped from the back of the animal until the shoes are on the feet of the person who wishes to wear them. That is a major thing in pushing costs higher and higher all the time.
I have here a statement that was made a few days ago in reference to this matter of costs involved in doing business today, which affects adversely the cost of living. The statement is made by a man who for over forty years was engaged in a certain line of business. He gives a table showing the approximate cost of doing business in 1947 compared with the cost of doing business in 1914 in a field in which, he states, he has had long experience. In 1947 materials cost him $1 and in 1914, fifty cents. Labour in 1947 cost him $4 as compared with
$1.50 in 1914. Overhead cost $1 in 1947, and in 1914 it cost fifty cents, while advertising in 1947 cost $1 as compared with fifty cents in 1914. In 1947 profit was $1 and in 1914, fifty cents. The total of these basic costs in 1947 was $8 as compared with $3.50 in 1914. He goes on. to say that if you add the excise tax of sixty-four cents, which in 1914 did not exist, you have $8.64 in 1947. Then add jobber's profit of twenty per cent, which in 1947 was $1.73 and in 1914, fifty-three cents, and add retailer's profits of fifty per cent which in 1947 was $5.18 as compared with $1.34 in 1914, and you have a total of $15.55 up to that point, in 1947. Then add a luxury tax of twenty-five per cent now imposed on this line-$3.88 of an increase-and the provincial tax of four per cent, making eighty cents, and you have a total of $20.23 in 1947 as compared with $5.37 in 1914.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: Part of that is profit.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Of course it is. But remember, Mr. Speaker, when you compute the hidden taxes added at the various levels and realize that a man has .to invest his money in the total cost of the article and carry it as inventory sometimes as long as six or seven months to meet the seasonal demands, you cannot blame him for taking a reasonable profit on his whole outlay. What else can you expect? Some people do not know business, nor do they appreciate what businessmen have to put up with in this day. Certainly it ought to be perfectly evident that if we are to tackle successfully the high cost of living and the high cost of doing business, we must be thinking in other terms than check-reins and controls. We have to begin thinking of freeing enterprise from the shackles and manacles that have bound it. When we talk about freeing enterprise that is what we Social Crediters mean. We mean freeing enterprise from the shackles of taxation and the manacles and check-reins imposed by the government. Give business reasonable opportunity, and at the same time see to it that the people themselves have in their hands purchasing power with which to buy. That is the best kind of control I know of.
I do not think I need labour further the point of taxation, but one other point I should like to mention is this. It was not a difficult thing during the war for the government to make an agreement with the milk producers of Canada whereby these producers furnished the consumers with milk at ten cents a quart. The producers were perfectly satisfied. We had no difficulty during the months in which the compensated price was in effect.

speechtext: Yes, we had.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
That is a matter that has to be shown. I was in the production of milk at the time and I knew something about it. I know how pleased generally the people were with that type of control. It certainly was not a difficult matter. The producers did furnish milk at ten cents a quart, but they themselves obtained thirteen cents for it. The simple method was that at the end of the month when I, for example, had finished my deliveries for that month I took into the local bank a statement of the number of quarts of milk I had distributed during that period. The bank checked this statement, and if it was reasonable in comparison with the one for the previous month, they stamped it as accepted and credited my bank account with two cents. We got another one cent per quart through subsidy. They then made up statements containing all such transactions and sent them back to the department in Ottawa. The statements were checked through and the banks were reimbursed out of the general revenue fund.
That may not be completely, but it is essentially, what took place. The people of the country immediately sensed the importance of that milk subsidy type of price control and they all reacted well to it. There was not a great deal of pressure to take it off; as a matter of fact there was more pressure to keep it on. Furthermore, under the system the people were enabled to buy more milk; andi because they could buy more, the demand increased and more milk was produced. The natural consequence was that during those months neither I nor most other producers could keep up with the demand. We could not get enough cows to do that. However, we did succeed in distributing a great deal more milk than would otherwise have been distributed, and the people did consume a great deal more than they would otherwise have consumed. The cost of administration. and the cost of the subsidy bonus, were certainly justified during those months.
Immediately the bonuses and subsidies were taken off. down went the consumption of milk all over Canada, and it has not. got back, and will not get back for many months, to what it was during the time of the subsidy. Subsidy, coupled with compensated price discount, did control effectively the price of milk to the consumers, and it could be used

with a great many other items just as successfully. The administrative problem in regard thereto is one which it is quite within our ability to cope with.
If you add to the foregoing proposal an approach to a new financial outlook, you may make it possible for the people of the country to save each year about half the amount which the government is taking from them by way of indirect, taxes. Canadians have to pay about $470 million odd a year in interest on the debt. In this you have another very important item in the cost, of living. Year after year, decade after decade, the government. has insisted upon retaining an outmoded financial structure that has to be crutched up and bolstered up periodically by just such things as the government is asking today, that is, emergency controls. We have constantly advocated this: we say if the government can mint and print twelve per cent of the money of this country as it is now doing, and see that it is distributed with no debt attached to it at its source, then it can mint and print and put figures in the books to the extent of 100 per cent of the money we have to use. Thus it would save this country the huge burden of interest that attaches to a system under which the government has to go to the banks and borrow eighty-eight per cent of the money the people use. We think the present is a stupid arrangement. As one means of tackling the cost of living, we have constantly advocated that a debt-free money structure be introduced in this country, which would immediately make possible a reduction of taxes, reflecting itself in the revenues we have to take from the people, of at least twenty-five per cent of the total revenues of this country this year. Surely, if we have to take such huge quantities of money from the people by way of taxes because of a money system that creates debt all along the way, we are bound to cause a serious increase in the cost of living.
So I say to you, Mr. Speaker, introduction of a debt-free money system is one of the proposals which, coupled with the proposals for subsidies, compensated price discounts, reduced taxes, would provide us with a set of automatic controls, as an alternative to the bureaucratic type of controls which we have today and which the C.C.F. has advocated so ardently over the years.
But let me repeat, nothing in this world will do more to meet the high cost of living than to tackle the cost of production right at the point where that cost is being, pressured up; I say that point is high taxation of the indirect type. When we come to understand that, then our best efforts- will be directed

Transitional Measures Act
toward leaving in the hands of the Canadian people more purchasing power, more of the products of their own labour, and. thus we shall increase their incentive to produce; we shall increase the happiness of the people; we shall give them a better weapon with which they themselves can control the cost of living.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is not a new idea to advocate that the people themselves are the best controllers; certainly it is not a new idea to advocate that the best way in the world to make it possible for the people themselves to control prices and the cost of living is for them to have in their hands at all times sufficient purchasing power with which to buy all the goods they have produced if they want them. Our present financial system does not do that. Over a long period our industrial system has resulted in the distribution of less purchasing power than the people needed to buy the goods they produced That is one of the principal reasons we had to have such things as are being suggested today; that is why we have had to have the most favoured-nation clauses, and Bretton Woods in trade treaties.

Yes, and war. The simple fact of the matter is, that internal pressure to get rid of goods that are in surplus-not surplus above what the people want and can use but surplus above what the people can buy-is one of the greatest causes for the necessity for these bureaucratic or planned controls.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us take a positive attitude toward these things and think in terms of abundance. Social Crediters have always been apostles of abundant living, not restricted living. We think that inherent within the whole system we suggest, which is a way or philosophy of life, we have a means by which, if it is introduced into Canada gradually over a period of two or three years, it would become possible for the government gradually also to do away with the type oi controls they use now, and introduce into Canada once more, a free way of living, which would confirm every man in his own rights.
I do not intend to take more time to go into our philosophy, because that is not what this resolution calls for. However, these fellows over here always ask questions about these matters, and drive a person into making explanations. Let me say that there is plenty of material available for them to read. I would suggest that they read the speeches and writings and follow the advice of my good friend the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) who, a few years ago certainly showed to all and sundry what can be done by way of introducing a system of controls, under the
social credit system, that will get rid of the shackles and the check-reins that have brought people down to a mentality of scarcity.
In closing, let me say once more that we will support the minister and give him another three months. What we will do after that time we do not know; it will depend upon the situation that then exists. But do not let it ever be said in this house or out on the hustings by anybody that we have pressured the government to throw off at once all their controls. That is stupid; it is not right. ' We think controls will be necessary for a time, but we object to the kind of control that is applied.

Order. I have always followed the practice that when two members rise at the same time, I should attempt to-give a chance to every party in the house to-speak; one after the other, of course. Now we would seem to be starting over again and, since no hon. member in the Liberal' party has risen, I believe the floor should be given to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker).

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend on this occasion to deal at length with the address to continue the act because the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has indicated that the three months extension is not going to be opposed in view of the fact that, had this session not been called at the present time, the Transitional Measures Act would have continued in any event to March 31, 1948.
For a moment or two, I shall review something of the background of this act. I have in my hand the original measure which indicates the degree to which in recent years this government has developed a passion for power, which, like greed, has shown that it is not capable of being satisfied.
I believe the people of Canada generally thought that, after the war, so far as possible the abrogation of our rights in wartime would be denied in days of peace. As I view the attitude of the government, I ask myself if it intends that the temporary abrogations of wartime, the paths which were taken in time of war, shall become the permanent highways of peace.
I think no more outrageous deception of a House of Commons was ever perpetrated than in the stand taken by the foreign exchange control board with the knowledge and direction of the government, to use powers given to the government for certain purposes and with the assurance by the government to the House of Commons that those powers would be used only for the purpose indicated, only to find that, in November of 1947 the powers thus secured are utilized, under a pretence, in order to effect the wielding of a power the board was never intended to have.
I have before me some of the speeches delivered in 1934 by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) when he was referring to a

Transitional Measures Act
government taking unto itself certain powers and using them improperly. We who are on this side of the house are now faced by a government which, in its greed for power, and at the expense of the House of Commons, has gone farther than any other government in Canada ever dreamed of going in a time of war or peace, and almost as far, indeed if not actually as far, as the socialist government in Great Britain has gone.
Last vear on April 18, 1947, as reported at page 2190 of Hansard, the minister gave his imprimatur of disapproval to the acquiring of powers by any board and the utilizing of those powers for purposes other than those for which they were intended. On that occasion he said, referring to a board-
They know very well that nothing would be more shortsighted than for them to rely upon arbitrary sections, as a basis for the unwarranted exercise of authority.
Is .that not the situation today? Is that not what this government did on November 17, 1947? It used for another purpose altogether, and for one for which it had denied it would under any circumstances use them, powers which parliament had given to it. That is a serious situation. Instead of its making even a faint apology, all we have from the executive in that regard is a comtemptuous attitude toward the House of Commons. I say, sir, that when a government utilizes powers such as that in a way never contemplated by parliament, we have a right to ask that parliament and the country be given an explanation.
I know what the excuse will be:	Certain
bureaucrats decided they needed power. Certain bureaucrats believed that if they could twist the interpretion of certain sections they would secure that power.
