I shall not deal further with that question at this time because of the interruption by the Minister of Justice. I suggest that, having regard to the trend which is being followed by this government, the time has come when this house should ascertain just in what direction this country is going in so far as centralization is concerned.
I should like to mention a few matters which support the view that I hold, that the government is endeavouring deliberately to centralize power here in Ottawa to the detriment of the provinces under our federal system. Every now and then the government produces the doctrine of emergency as its authority. The doctrine of emergency was never intended to be utilized by any government to destroy the set-up of powers under the British North America Act and to deny the jurisdiction of the provinces. As far as this government is concerned, the doctrine of emergency has become a synonym for government incompetencv. Whenever the government is in doubt as to what move it should follow, it invariably adds powers to certain individuals or boards, relying upon the doctrine of emergency as justifying its acts.
Transitional Measures Act

Was it not the government that took the stand a few short months ago that the constitution of our country could be amended by the simple expedient of a majority in the House of Commons and the Senate? Was it not a member of this government, the former Minister of Justice, who stated that the language rights of the people in this country could be taken away by a simple majority in the House of Commons and the Senate? The statement made by the then Minister of Justice that the right to use the French language in this country could be denied by the simple expediency of a majority vote of the House of Commons and the Senate was one of the most dangerous statements that have ever been made in this house.
Let us see what they have done toward centralization. I would point out that they have this in common with my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party'. The C.C.F. party supported them in that because its members realize that they can never bring into being a system of socialism on a national scale until the constitution, in so far as provincial rights are concerned, has been entirely changed and those rights done away with.
It is a continuing process; the government is working in the direction of centralization. They wanted to take away from the provinces certain rights to tax; they wanted to centralize authority; they succeeded. The Premier of Nova Scotia stated that what he had done was done under pressure. The minister of public works of Alberta has stated that while his province consented, she consented only because of the compulsion of a gun held to her head. That is the pathway toward centralization. The doctrine of emergency is being used more and more as an excuse and means whereby provincial jurisdiction can be denied.
My hon. friends of the C.C.F. talk about how easy it is to control prices, and they have admitted that the responsibility for such control rests upon the provincial government under our constitution when and if the transitional powers act is done away with. I ask them, why was chapter 91 of the 1947 statutes of Saskatchewan passed? That is an act to confer certain powers upon the lieutenant governor in council, and the preamble reads:
Whereas, in contemplation of the termination of certain powers conferred upon the governor in council by the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, and of certain powers conferred by the governor in council pursuant to that act, it is expedient that the lieutenant governor in council be empowered, upon termination of any of the said powers, to do and authorize the doing of such acts and things and make such orders and regulations within the legislative competence of the province, as he

may deem necessary or advisable with respect to any or all of the matters hereinafter mentioned, namely-
(b)	controlling and regulating the prices at which goods, wares or merchandise or any class or classes thereof shall be purchased or sold by retail within the province or any part or parts of the province for use in the province;
(c)	controlling and regulating rentals of real property and the use and occupation of real property within the province-
Why was that act passed? It was passed because the law officers of thq crown in Saskatchewan realized that under the constitution, when the war was over, responsibility to control prices and the like was within the ambit of the province. I am not saying anything against their commendable efforts to secure reasonable prices in this country because I think all of us are opposed to inflationary tendencies, but I ask them this: When you have it in your power, when you have such an overwhelming majority- in the province, why do you not carry into effect in Saskatchewan the principles that you avow here in the House of Commons?
That is what we are doing with lumber.

Yes, it is being done with lumber and that may be the reason why it is not being done with anything else. The man who works, the man who produces lumber is receiving from $22 to $25 less per thousand feet than the man under private enterprise in the adjoining provinces is receiving.
You would remove the means of maintaining the ceilings.

That remark is
scarcely worthy of so good a member as the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). What I am saying is this. They have the law, and all that it requires is a proclamation. How they have proclaimed their belief in controlled prices! I ask them when they reply to answer this question: Why do you not do it in Saskatchewan where you have the power to do it, not only under the constitution, but also under the statute passed for the purpose?
The act cannot be implemented while the emergency powers act is in operation.

There is nothing to stop a province from utilizing its powers. We have not come to the state where the transitional powers act has taken away the rights of a province to legislate. The province has legislated, and if you believe that the province of Saskatchewan can control prices, here is your opportunity to carry into effect that

Transitional Measures Act
great philosophic experiment. I am going to help them answer the question because I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) this afternoon answered the question himself. Did you notice, Mr. Speaker, how he went over with great speed-I think the word is "elided"-the difference in prices between Canada and the United States? He pointed out by inference how difficult it is for people of this country to maintain a price level lower than the price level that maintains across the boundary, and I presume that would be the situation were the government of Saskatchewan to bring into effect its system of price control.
I say this to the government. I have heard the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the most lachrymose words point out the evils of combines and exploitation. I remember the words that went over the radio on election night in 1935, when the Prime Minister declared what a great victory it was for those who were opposed to great monopoly privilege. How many prosecutions have there been? How many times have the powers been used against monopolies? If there are corporations in this country that take unfair advantage and exploit the people I say to my friends of the C.C.F. that last year I moved an amendment whereby any man or woman in this country, where there is exploitation or unfairness, could lay an information in the courts of this country. Have they done it?
Yes.

One lone sound, and an uncertain one at that. The only prosecution that is even discussed is of the dental manufacturers at a time when so many say that unfair exploitation is sapping the energy of the people of this country. Go into the courts.
What will it cost the individual?

What does it cost? My hon. friend's party have in their midst one of the ablest counsel, the learned and hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke). Ask him. That is where to get the information. My hon. friends to my left used to claim that it was unfair that prosecutions could take place only with the leave of the Attorney General of Canada or the attorneys general of the several provinces and that they were leagued together with great interests who unfairly took advantage of the people. But no longer is that excuse available. When wrong is done, let it be punished. Where exploitation takes place, my hon. friends have it in their power to carry into effect the principles which they publicly avow.
You know, sir, that the first move of a socialist in order to bring in a socialist economy-andi sometimes as I look at the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie)
I wonder how he feels at being an instrument for bringing in socialism in our country-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Very proud of it.
If the hon. member for Lake Centre would permit a question, would he tell us how a Tory would bring in anything?
What a clever question!
Sir, the quality of that question answers itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I may have the privilege of answering the question that my hon. friend asked of me as to how I feel about helping to bring socialism into Canada, I would say that were I in charge tomorrow and had to choose between Socialism and a rigid and unbending Toryism I would prefer socialism.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister should have got married twenty years ago.
Mr. Speaker, I have never known so many trying to make one speech. I do say to my right hon. friend that all his life as long as I have known him he has been honourable and never right.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am glad that my hon. friend did not say that I was right and never honourable.
That is something I would not say. But I did point out that he had never been right.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He has never lost an election in thirty years, which is more than my hon. friend can say.

My right hon.
friend has told us that he does believe in the principles of socialism-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do very largely.

-and I thank him for that, because no other government has ever gone so far in the direction of socialism anywhere as the present government, and we now have the admission of the right hon. house leader of his general attitude toward socialism. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will make some allowance in- the time allotted to me because of the general interest that is being shown in my speech.
I now come to the next point. The essence of socialism and bringing it into effect is a denial of the right of appeal of the individual to the courts against the arbitrary acts of bureaucrats.
Transitional Measures Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Nonsense.

This government has gone a long way under its powers in the transitional powers act to deny the individual the right of recourse to the courts. A few weeks ago the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) came back from Britain. He spoke in the city of Toronto and in scathing tones condemned the socialist government in Great Britain for placing power in the hands of one man. Now this government is going to ask parliament to'place in the hands of the Minister of Reconstruction, who has never shown a scrupulous regard for parliamentary procedure, power over every individual in this country; the power to say to one industry, "You shall live"; and to another, "You shall die"; to one, "You shall receive"; to another, "You shall be denied." And no one who is affected, whether by way of discrimination or otherwise, is permitted recourse to the courts. Sir, where will freedom be when one individual in this country is given powers the like of which no one has possessed since the days of Oliver Cromwell?
What about Cripps?
I have heard a statement of Cripps' powers. They do not go as far as those which are to repose in the hands of the Minister of Reconstruction.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is not such a good man.

What was that
remark? He is a good man? Somebody said long before anyone of us was here that power corrupts, but absolute power corrupts absolutely.
And how!

Yes. Place that
power in his hands, place any member in that cabinet in a position where he is above the courts of the land, where he can divide the Canadian people into two groups-those who shall receive and those who shall be denied- be he ever so good, without right of recourse to the courts against unfairness and discrimination, and you deny the basic principles of all the Liberalism for which my right hon friend, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) has so often stood and so generally and vocally avowed. It is exactly the same principle that we have today under socialism in the province of Saskatchewan. They interfere with the individual, and in their statutes they place these words:
Every order of the board under this section shall be 'final and without appeal, and no such [DOT]order shall be questioned or reviewed, restrained

or removed by prohibition, injunction, certiorari, or any other process or proceeding in any court.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Compare that with the Marketing Act of the Tory government in 1935.

Never at any time has any government outside of the socialist government asked to be above the courts of the land. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Kindersley, for whose constitutional knowledge I have a deep regard, last year introduced in the house a bill to provide for the doing away of appeals to the privy council. That was a move. Will he introduce it again this year? I never heard such silence as an answer.
Oh, oh.
Mr. Frank R. Scott, one of the leaders of the C.C.F., the president of the association-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is a good man.
And he is a professor.

Mr. Scott said why the appeal to the privy council should be retained, in the Canadian Bar Review of June-July, 1947. At the same time as the hon. member for Kindersley was abolishing the appeal, Mr. Scott was giving reason why it should be retained. And do you know what the reason is, sir? It was this. We have a socialist government in England today and it appoints some of the members to the privy council, so we may expect favourable consideration of the policies of socialism if we maintain the appeal to the privy council.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not worthy of the hon. member at all.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I shall introduce the bill.

All right. Here is
what Mr. Scott says:
In recent years a new argument in support of tlie appeal has appeared.
I read this article because it indicates a dangerous principle. Under their legislation there is a denial of recourse to the courts, because the individual has no right of recourse. The article continues:
England has now embarked upon a great socialist experiment, and one which, because it seeks to preserve the democratic process, may have a more profound repercussion upon the world than even the Russian revolution. The judicial committee of the privy council lives, breathes and operates in that social climatP The Canadian supreme court, on the other hand, is engulfed in the tide of post-war reaction which is now running strongly in North America, Canada included. So far from experimenting

Transitional Measures Act
afresh, we are scrapping and undoing the public enterprises and social controls which were necessary to win the war, and which raised our productivity and standard of living to unprecedented heights.
Then he goes on to say:
Which of these two courts is the more likely to render the better service to the democratic cause in these future conflicts?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask a question of my hon. friend?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Which does my hon. friend favour?
He does not know.

At the moment I am pointing out that the one reason why the appeal to the privy council was to be taken away was to ensure Canadian sovereignty. On the other hand, there is the argument now used by one of the great leaders of the C.C.F. that possibly it would be worth maintaining because the court might, by reason of its proximity to the social changes taking place in Britain, in consequence give a better interpretation than the Supreme Court of Canada. I say, sir, that is a dangerous principle. Afraid of the courts? Today the government of our country too often has been afraid of the courts. Too often, under the legislation passed under the transitional powers act, has the right of the individual who is discriminated against been denied; too often and too long.
I do not think the hon. member mentioned the book from which he was quoting.
It is the Canadian Bar Review.
What page?
June-July, 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I should like to ask a question. My recollection was that Mr. Scott came to the conclusion nevertheless that the appeal should be abolished in spite of that.
I have the whole article here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may be wrong.

Apparently the
Minister of Justice has not read that article with his usual care.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Maybe not. But that is the impression I got.

I will read the Minister what the article says:
These are weighty questions. The answers given will often depend on the ideological preferences of the individual concerned.
Then, as it is fair to point out, he goes on to say what my hon. friend said:
Yet no such considerations, in my opinion justify the retention of the appeal.
Oh, oh.

I do not make any apology. That is the argument that was
advanced-
Go on.
That was the argument advanced.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is unworthy of a member of parliament.

-no right of appeal because the rights would be denied to individuals here in Canada under social legislation; and very fairly, as the Minister of Justice points out-and I read it-he went on finally to say that in his opinion-
The hon. member was compelled to read it.

-the appeal should be done away with. . That indicates a philosophy of suspicion and fear of the courts which underlies the attitude taken by this government in denying the right of appeal to the courts, and I say to you, sir, that these are the trends-centralization, legislative centralization and taxation centralization; then the interference with provincial jurisdiction and the denying of the right of recourse to the courts, which I say cannot be justified. No emergency such as exists today should permit of denial of recourse.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice that when this bill is introduced it should provide for recourse to the courts, and before we proceed we should have the right to bring before the house and the members of this house those who occupy high positions in the bureaucratic service of the country, with a view to having them tell us what justification there ever is for departing from the constitutional principle that taxation shall not be imposed except through the House of Commons, a principle never departed from before. No reason has been given for it, and I ask the government to give the people of the country the assurance that never again will they depart from the promise they made that under no circumstances would they allow the people of this country to be subjected to regulations interpreted differently from the way in which they were interpreted in parliament, but that they will restore to the people the freedom denied them during the period of the war.
Transitional Measures Act

As far as this party is concerned, it believes the time has come to restore the flag of freedom to parliament hill once and for all.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE WITH RESPECT TO ASSISTANCE TO INDUSTRY

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE WITH RESPECT TO ASSISTANCE TO INDUSTRY
speechtext:
With your permission, Mr. Speaker,
I wish to make a brief statement.
For some time the Canadian government has been considering its proposal to grant assistance to the gold mining industry. Representations have been received from the industry to the effect that the government's proposal, which I announced in my broadcast address on November 17 last, would not serve to prevent continued deterioration of the industry, the closing down of additional mines and consequent hardship to many northern mining communities.
Furthermore, as I stated in that broadcast, Canada has certain obligations under the international monetary fund agreement which have to be taken into account in considering the form in which any assistance is given to the industry. It was for that reason and in order to give an opportunity to discuss the matter with the international monetary fund that our original proposal was announced only in general terms, with the statement that details would not be made known until they were laid before parliament. During the last fortnight the government has been in consultation with the fund. In the course of these discussions it developed that payment of a fixed amount per extra ounce of gold produced had, from the fund's point of view, certain objectionable features in that it might be' represented as constituting an increase in the price paid by the government for gold which would be contrary to the fund agreement. The government has therefore decided to revise the form of its assistance and I wish now to give an outline of our new proposal, which the government hopes will contribute in some degree to the reconstitution of our depleted gold reserves.
Under the new proposal the government will undertake to make through the Department of Mines and Resources a payment to each gold mine designed to assist it in defraying part of its increased costs of production. This
[Mr. DiefenbakerJ
payment will be determined by taking half of the amount by which the mine's current cost of gold production per fine ounce exceeds SIS per ounce and applying this to the amount by which production in the current year exceeds two-thirds of production in .the base year; that is, the twelve months' period ending June 30, 1947. In the case of new mines, the payment as described above will be paid on the entire production in the first year and in the two succeeding years on the amount by which current production exceeds two-thirds of the first year's production. The legislation will include definitions of such terms as cost of production and will limit the assistance to straight gold mines rather than include those metal mines which produce gold as a byproduct. The assistance will be given for a term of three years and will apply to production after December 1, 1947.
I may add that the details of the proposal will be incorporated in legislation to be submitted to the house as soon as practicable.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General praying that the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, be continued in force until the 31st day of March, 1948.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is not in his seat at the moment because I wish to reply briefly to some of the statements he made this afternoon. I thought the speech he delivered did not display the integrity and quality generally shown in this house by the hon. gentleman. Since he comes from western Canada and has probably absorbed some of the thinking out there-what I might call the advanced thinking-on economics and other questions, I thought he might have expressed a different viewpoint. However, this afternoon in my estimation he exhibited three typical Tory characteristics. First, he spoke for some forty-five minutes- and did not state his position on the matter he was discussing. He did not say whether he was going to vote in favour of the measure or against it. Probably he will do as his party has done on previous occasions; that is, talk consistently against the measure and then vote for it.
Then the hon. member deliberately tried to leave a wrong impression with the house and the country with respect to the opinions of the chairman of the Co-operative Common-

Transitional Measures Act
wealth Federation. I believe that is beneath the dignity and ability the hon. member for Lake Centre usually displays in this house. When he did not succeed in that he tried to leave an entirely wrong impression with regard to certain legislation passed by the Saskatchewan legislature. Then he exhibited the usual Tory fetish for procedure and precedent. I am sure that, had the Tories remained in power in England up to the present time, and carried on as the hon. gentleman did this afternoon, in that country they would probably still be hanging men for stealing sheep.
We are living in a changed world today, in a world dynamic in its ability to destroy and also in its ability to produce. The measure we are discussing here is a measure of control, 'a measure which we consider necessary to secure greater production of the essential things of life. Many people have said in this house and in the country that you can get production only through a completely free economy, in which free enterprise has full control. If we learned anything at all from the war we should have learned that this is false. In 1939, when the war broke out, we had a national production of goods and services in Canada worth approximately $4,250 million. When war came we realized it was absolutely essential that we increase that production. We knew we would have to place from half a million to a million of our young men and women in the armed forces and that we would have to equip them with proper clothing, medical services and all the other things necessary to win a war. To do that, our government realized, thank goodness, that certain controls were essential, and they imposed those controls for the purpose of getting greater production in order to carry on Canada's war effort. And I may say that we can be exceedingly proud of Canada's war effort. We equipped that army with the best equipment in the world; and during the four or more years of the war we were able to give away a billion dollars worth of goods and services each year, all because we had adopted the controls necessary to bring about production in this country of those things that were essential.
Now we say we are going to get rid of these controls. I say the emergency is almost as great today as it was during the war. We have not yet won the peace. Anyone who looks at world conditions must realize that production is almost as essential today as it was during the war years; and the objective of these controls is to obtain the necessary essential production. If we could produce to the extent we did during 1944 and 1945, when 5849 -13J
we produced some $12,000 million worth of goods and services, surely we can continue that production now with 800,000 of our most productive young people back at work producing goods and services for ourselves and for the people of Europe who find themselves unable to produce because of the war.
These are the objectives of controls; this is why they are necessary at the present time. Yet there are people who would throw them out the window. I cannot understand the mentality of such people. It is very true that no government can give its people more than those people produce, but it is equally true that the government of a democratic country should give its people the opportunity to produce, and should see that when they have produced there is an equitable distribution of the goods and services so produced. That is what is needed in Canada today-greater production of certain essential goods and services, goods and services which will give to our veterans returning from overseas decent homes to live in and which will give to our people the goods and services which we can supply in this country.
How did' we get that increased production during the war? We got it because we, for the first time in this country, established a reasonable relationship between wages, the price of agricultural products and the cosits of the things which we had to buy. When that balance was established we got greater production than at any time in Canada's history. We produced more hogs and more milk; we produced more of all those essential things; and we got for the first time a reasonably fair distribution of them. I am not saying it was perfect; nothing is perfect in this world. But, looking back over the past forty years, I think any member in the house will agree with me that during 1944 and 1945 we had probably a better distribution of the goods and services we produce in this country than we had at any time previously. And as a result of that we got -production of all the essential things in life.
Now we find that just as we get rid of those controls we have a decrease in production. What is happening in the agricultural industry today, so far as production is concerned? What is happening with production of bacon, production of dairy products and the production of practically all agricultural products? Once that fair relationship between the cost of production and the price received for farm products is distributed, and where you have that disparity, immediately you get a decrease in production.
This party has never said that you can give people something for nothing. But you can
Transitional Measures Act

give the people an opportunity to produce by maintaining in this country a proper balance between wages and the price of agricultural products, and the things we have to buy. That is all we mean when we speak of a planned economy. We mean an economy in which those relationships are maintained, in which we get the maximum production and thereby give to more people more goods and services.
The minute you return to the speculative system, that balance is destroyed. Today the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) talked about rye. He spoke about the price of rye, but he did not tell the whole story. He did not tell that the processors of rye used for food purposes in this country bought that rye at sixty-six cents a bushel. That was the ceiling price on rye in 1941, and the price paid for rye used for food purposes in this country. There was speculation on the Winnipeg grain exchange. The difference between sixty-six cents and t'he speculative price created by the Winnipeg grain exchange was paid out of the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada. I think I am right in that. Rye used for the production of food in this country was bought at a ceiling price established in 1941. No wonder they could speculate on the Winnipeg grain exchange, when the man who was processing the rye did not care what he paid for it if it was processed for food purposes, because he could pay what he liked for it on the Winnipeg grain exchange and the government paid a subsidy representing the difference between that and sixty-six cents a bushel. That is something which I do not think the people of this country realized. It was subsidized speculation on the Winnipeg grain exchange.
Our hon. friends to the right have stated that 'they 'believe that the two systems could work again, namely the speculative system and the wheat board, or the marketing board. I say they cannot work when you have longterm agreements for the sale of your products. Those long-term agreements cannot be filled wi'th two systems in Canada.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: They can be filled with jne system.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
They can be filled to the 2xtent that we produce those goods in this 30untry; make no mistake about that. That is why we believe 'that we should have the necessary controls. That is why we believe that the Winnipeg grain exchange should be closed and all speculation on essential food produots should be stopped. If we do not do that there is no doubt in my mind that we diall return again to 'the completely speculative marketing system in this country.

Our hon. friends say that the cause of discontent, if there is discontent in western Canada at the present time with regard to the price received for grain, is the failure of the government to allow grain prices to rise. I say the greater part of the discontent in western Canada today is due to the failure of the government to maintain controls necessary to prevent the rising cost of production in that part of the country.
Immediately controls were taken off binder twine, for instance, it went up to twice the price it had been before. When the subsidy was taken off crude oil the price went up; and the same is true with respect to farm machinery. The western Canadian farmer will receive for his wheat, I believe, over the five-year period of the contract with Great Britain, probably $1.70 or $1.75 a bushel.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: What would he 'have got if there had been no control?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Nobody in the world knows what he might have got if there had been no control; with 160,000,000 bushels additional grain on the world market, nobody can tell what might have happened. But I will tell you this, that if the controls had been maintained over the cost of production the western farmers would have been very well satisfied with SI.70 to $1.75 a bushel; I am convinced of that.
It is with respect to the removal of controls over the western farmer's cost of production that most dissatisfaction is expressed in western Canada. There are people who put the cart before the horse and who turn it the other way around. But I am saying this, that, after all, the western farmer is a pretty sensible person. He knows which side his bread is buttered on, and I have no doubt as to what his reaction will be to this outcry by the Winnipeg grain exchange or the Progressive Conservative party to my right, and certain other interests, who would put him back into the speculative market again, so far as his farm production is concerned.
In respect of agriculture in Canada we want stability so that we can plan our agricultural program, not just for one year, but for four or five years. Every control which has been removed has been a step in the direction of instability-not stability.	That is why I say
that we are getting a decrease in production in Canada, so far as agricultural prices are concerned.
I should like to deal briefly with what has happened in respect of coarse grains. When the Canadian Wheat Board Act was before the house last session we in this house endeavoured at first to have coarse grains placed under that

Transitional Measures Act
act, and have the price of coarse grains placed at a figure in relation to the price of wheat. Anyone who has farmed must know approximately what that relationship should be. If that had been done we would not have found the sorry spectacle which developed in western Canada when these ceilings were removed. It has been said in eastern Canada that they were removed because of the demands of western agriculture. That is not so. It was not because of the demands of western agriculture that these ceilings were removed. Mr. Speaker, you should have been in western Canada and heard the outcry raised out there when that happened. In fact they had to call the Liberal association of Saskatchewan together at a special meeting and the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), who is parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and another gentleman were sent to Ottawa to interview the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the government with regard to it, although the Minister of Agriculture was in western Canada when it happened. I do not know why they felt that they had to send them to Ottawa. They must have more money in their treasury than we of the C.C.F. have!

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: That is quite a bit.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
I wish it were more. That is the position. The western farmer had already sold. It was said that we were refusing to sell our grain, but the statistics show that over 50,000,000 bushels of coarse grains had been marketed before the ceiling came off. Those coarse grains had not reached the consumer in eastern Canada; they were still either in the hands of the handling firms and speculators or in transit. Thank goodness we have a pool organization out there and a large portion of those coarse grains was in their hands. The result is that the producers of those grains who are members of the pool will get some return as a result of the increase in the price. We do not know what it will be because we do not know how much had been disposed of before the ceiling came off.
The hon. member for Rosthern returned to western Canada and announced the government policy in the press, or what the government were likely to do with regard to the whole coarse grains business. I do not know when he became the official mouthpiece of the government. He may have just been talking out of turn or expressing his hope as to what they would do. That situation is not satisfactory, either to the western producer or to the eastern farmer who consumes these grains.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: What did he say?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
I shall not go into the details of what he said, but he said plenty, perhaps more than he should have said. We want stability in these prices. If these grains had been placed under the wheat board, as we suggested then, for at least the life of the wheat board we would have known where these prices were going. That would have been the situation up until 1950 at least. Then the eastern consumer would have been able to plan a fairly substantial feeding program. But that did not take place and we now have complete disorganization in our whole agricultural livestock production system.
There is another matter to be dealt with, the subsidies on freight rates. Hon. friends to my right do not believe in subsidies. What is going to happen in the latter part of July next year when the subsidies on coarse grains freight rates are taken off? We shall find ourselves back in the position in which we were in 1939 and we shall be exporting our coarse grains to the Scandinavian countries at from five to seven cents a bushel less than the feeders in eastern Canada can buy them for. That was the position in 1939 because of the differential between the export freight rates and the domestic freight rates on grain. If there is an increase of even half what the railroads are asking that differential will be even more than from five to seven cents a bushel. We shall then be supplying the Scandinavian countries with feed grain so that they can compete with us in the British market. We shall be supplying those grains more cheaply than we can sell them in eastern Canada or the maritime provinces.
That is the sort of thing that happens when you refuse to provide necessary returns in order to maintain a balanced economy in the country. That is the ultimate result of the decontrol policy. I ask my Progressive Conservative friends to go out and explain that to their constituents in this province and hear what they have to say. I know enough of the eastern farmer and feeder in Ontario and the maritimes-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one occasion on which I feel very proud to belong to a peaceful race. I do not have to scrap, as many of those who have spoken this afternoon have done. I intend to speak for only a short time because some of my colleagues will be entering the debate later.
While the people of Britain and Europe continue to face months of slow starvation, the government of Canada continues to enforce its program of restricted production on our farms, even though it has contracted with the British government to supply special specified minimum quantities of wheat, 'beef, pork and other farm products. Although a policy of decreased production has been in effect generally since the early years of the war, the government continues from time to time to bring in measures that have the direct or indirect effect of reducing production. For that reason I feel that the farmers of this country are compelled to cut their production to the bone or, in some cases, work themselves out of business. That situation does not obtain in any other occupational group in this country, and something should be done in the very near future to remedy the situation with respect to our farmers.
Not very long ago the government announced the policy of decontrol of the prices of oats and barley and at the same time, I believe, removed the control from meats. In my opinion this has caused more discontent and unrest among the farmers of western Canada than anything else that has been done for many years.
We know that in the past agriculture has not had a square deal. Time and again we have stated from this corner of the house that you cannot have poverty and prosperity side by side in this country and at the same time have a contented population. We believe, as I have stated on many occasions, that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada and that, until we have a prosperous agriculture, the country as a whole cannot be prosperous. In order to bring this home to the
government, we have from time to time pointed out injustices, which so far have not been remedied.
Agriculture during many years has not received its proper share of the national income. During the war agriculture was asked to produce to the limit and succeeded in doing that very thing. We were told during the early years of the war that if we would be satisfied to accept low prices for our agricultural products we would be compensated when the war was over. The war was concluded in 1945, the shooting part at least, but up to the present time we have not yet fully realized those better times that were promised to agriculture.
Prices of coarse grains were controlled up to October 22, when the controls were removed. The immediate effect was an incease in price of twenty cents on oats and thirty cents on barley. Farmers all over the prairie provinces-and this applied, I think, just as much to eastern Canada and the mari-times-protested against this action of the government. Many farmers during the war years had made preparations for raising hogs on a large scale, but because of the increase in the price of feed many of them have now gone out of business or almost gone out of business and action will have to' be taken immediately if this situation is to be remedied. Perhaps it is even now too late to correct the situation because, during the past weeks, thousands of sows which should be farrowing in the winter months have been sent to the packing houses and many others which should be producing young pigs in the spring months have also gone .to the slaughter house. They cannot be brought back, and for that reason I feel that we are going to have a greatly decreased hog production in Canada next year. We have food contracts with Britain. I understand that the British people are now rationed and allowed only one ounce of bacon a week. If we are to do our share in helping those people we must get busy right away.
At the time the price ceilings on oats and barley were removed another strange thing happened. Those grains were allowed to be sold on the Winnipeg grain exchange. The vast majority of members on all sides of the house have urged the government for many years past to do away with the grain exchange. Some members of the government time and again have insisted that they are not in favour of the exchange. But we know that for years past they have also stated that they were going to reform the other part of this parliament, and we see from time to time that more and more leeway is given in ceitain directions.

crop year. That would be only fair to the farmers who delivered in accordance with the policy laid down by the government. It is within the rights of the farmers who made early delivery that this action should be taken, and farmers should be assured in the near future that such action will be taken.
Next, I would suggest a transfer from general revenue to the Canadian wheat board of an amount equal to the difference between the amounts realized under the British wheat agreement and the average world price received during each crop year.
Finally, I would suggest that there be provided an increase in the price of cattle and hogs, by subsidy or otherwise, so that the price would bear a fair relationship to the price of feed grains. I am making this statement at the present time on behalf of my group, and we shall have more to say later on.

speechtext:
I believe the people of Canada, from coast to coast, would be surprised if they had been able to attend in this House of Commons during the last two days and see how lightly this question of the cost of living has been treated so far on the government side of the house. Listening to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) speaking the other day on the question of-price control, I was amazed at the most unsatisfactory and disapponiting message he delivered in this house for us to take home with us at Christmas, if we do go home. About all he could tell us, as far as I could see in Hansard, was contained in the statement recorded on page 95, in which he said that this government was watching carefully what the government of the United States was proposing to do about price control. These are his words:
The present intention of the government is, as hon. members know, to ask for an extension of the powers which now exist to impose and maintain price controls for a further period.
And here is the significant part of his statement:
I would hope that during that further period it will be possible for us to get a clearer idea of just what can be done in this field in the interests of the Canadian economy.
There you have a responsible minister of the crown, in whose hands the whole question was left, after all the discussion that has been carried on for the past two sessions, after all the representations that have been made by the people of Canada in between the two sessions, telling us in this parliament, at this stage, that the government is watching the

situation to see what the United States is going to do, and in the interim trying to decide what is best for the Canadian economy.
I suggest that the people who sent us here in all seriousness expect far more than that. I do not believe the people of Canada will be satisfied if we go home to them and report that having come to Ottawa and laid their representations before the government, having pointed out to the government the alarming increase in the cost of living, a minister of the crown has promised that he will watch the situation.
It appears that the official policy of the government is to wait and see. I think the people of Canada are entitled to more than a policy of wait and see.
What is the trend of the thinking of the Minister of Finance? What can we expect in that interim period when he is going to watch the United States government and wait and see? The indication is given on page 94 of Hansard, where we find his point of view on the whole question of controls. There he states:
Any system of over-all price control involves over-all detailed direction of the Canadian economy.
He went on to point out that, so far as he was concerned, he was not prepared to recommend to this house that we adopt such a system. That would leave the impression that if we did not have a system of price controls under the authority of the government, we would not have an over-all system of what he called directed economy.
May I point out to the members of the house something I have pointed out before in this house? It is a fallacy to say that if we remove the system of government price controls, which we have had, and which we have in a small measure now, we shall have a system of free enterprise in this country. I have made the statement before and I make it now, that we have never had a free enterprise system in this country ever since the country began, and there is plenty of evidence to bear that out. All one needs to do is to read the report prepared by the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act. There he will see plenty of evidence to show that the creation and development of monopolies and cartels in Canada, the United States and other countries, from the very beginning of our Canadian economy have made it absolutely impossible for free enterprise to operate. For example, at page 45 of his report for last year the commissioner said:
The participants in cartels often make use of patent rights to divide the markets of the

Transitional Measures Act
world among themselves by national territories and to establish within a national territory a comprehensive system of marketing control.
What does this mean? It means that the monopolies and cartels which make agreements among themselves supersede and override the decisions of national governments and make the operation of free enterprise and competition absolutely impossible. If that is the situation we face I think this government should do a great deal more than just wait and see as far as prices are concerned.
One matter that has been discussed by a great many hon. members so far is the effect of the removal of subsidies and ceilings on coarse grains which go into the feeding of livestock. I have in my hand a memorandum from the Manitoba Federation of Agriculture, which gives certain information as to the attitude of the farmers of that province. All the farm forums were asked what they thought about the removal of ceilings on coarse grains. The first question was, "What do you think of this action by the government?" One hundred per cent of those who replied were opposed to that action. That is a most unusual development among organized farmers right across the province, where one would expect a difference of opinion. In this case 100 per cent of those who replied to the question said they were opposed to that action. The alternative suggested was that coarse grains should be marketed through the Canadian wheat board, and there again 100 per cent of those who replied agreed to this suggestion. I believe that is something the government should take as a warning sign. Surely, if all the farmers who were sufficiently interested to answer this questionnaire agreed on these things, the government should swallow its pride for once, admit that it made a mistake and do something before it is too late.
The question also was asked, "How will it affect farming operations in your community in regard to grain for feed?" The answer by ninety per cent of those questioned was, "Grain will be sold for cash instead of being fed". The answer of eighty per cent was, "Grain production will be curtailed". Another question was, "How will it affect farm operations in your community in regard to the marketing of livestock?" Ninety per cent of those who answered said, "Animals are being killed or shipped unfinished". Eighty per cent replied, "Livestock production will be cut". Another question asked was, "How will it affect other farm plans?" Eighty per cent answered, "Confusion in respect of farm 5849-14J
operations". With answers of that kind coming from organized farming in one of our best agricultural provinces, the government should be convinced that it has made a very bad mistake.
Here are some typical quotations from the farm groups throughout the province in regard to the action of the government in placing coarse grains on the grain exchange. One was, "This action was a betrayal of our confidence and causes us to lose faith in the government". Another was, "Farmers are forced to cut livestock production, while there is still a shortage of food in Europe". Another was, "Farm plans have been disrupted". Most of them said, "We advocate the abolition of the grain exchange," and all agreed that they want stable markets in coarse grains as we now have in wheat.
Whatever may be said on the question of the wheat contract, there is not the slightest doubt that, as far as the organized farmers of the prairies are concerned, the principle of a guaranteed floor price sufficient to bring at least the cost of production, plus the prospect of an assured market over a period of years, has been definitely accepted; but unfortunately, through the action of the government, that principle has received a serious blow. I have before me a whole stack of resolutions from farm organizations and co-operatives in western Canada protesting the action of the government and asking that something be done immediately, first, to compensate those farmers who sold their coarse grains between the turn of the crop year and when the ceilings were removed, and, second, to do something to stabilize the price of feed grains so that livestock production might go ahead.
Returning to the question of price controls, which I was discussing a moment ago, if it were only the members of the opposition on this side of the house who thought profiteering was going on and that the cost of living was exorbitant, perhaps the government could say, "Well, members of the opposition are inclined to criticize the government for its actions at all times." But I have before me a reprint from the Ottawa Citizen of December 1, 1947, reporting a speech delivered in the city of Quebec by one of the members sitting on the government side of the house. I believe he describes himself as an independent Liberal, but he is a supporter of the present government. Among other things he is reported to have said:
A multitude of citizens are burdened with, exorbitant living costs while a handful of capitalists make exorbitant profits.
Transitional Measures Act

a whole page of advertising by one of the chartered banks, the International Nickel Company, General Motors or some other large corporation, telling in bold print just how wonderful the competitive system is. They start out with a slogan of some sort, something like, "Competition is the life of trade." But they do not tell you that it is the death of the trader. Then they go on to tell you how price levels can be automatically adjusted by giving free play to the competitive forces in our society. It all looks very good on paper, particularly when they use the taxpayers' money to pay for the advertisements. The money which they are using for advertising should go in as excess profits and be taxed, but they make use of the money of the people to put out propaganda in the interests of their own industry.
Then what do they do? They sell the idea of competition to the common man; they tell the working man, the farmer, the schoolteacher, the lawyer, the merchant, that he must compete with his fellow man and snatch bread1 from his hand's in order to live. Then they proceed to form co-operatives among themselves or monopolies or combines. I a.m not talking in any abstract way because I have before me the report of an investigation into dental supplies with which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) is familiar and in connection with which I understand some action is pending.
There is plenty of evidence that these same gentry who hand out this mulligan stew of competition and say it is good for us; refuse to practice competition because they know that it does not work. They found out long ago that throat-cutting competition does no one any good and so for themselves they form co-operatives or combines or whatever you want to call it. They get together once in a while to set the prices of things they sell. I do not mind people forming a combine or a monopoly if they are honest about it, but I object when they deliberately try to befuddle the public by teaching competition, by teaching them that the only way to become prosperous is by tramping down on your neighbour, that the only thing is the free-for-all system like the elephant dancing with the chickens, which is pretty good for the elephant. Then they pool together to control the prices, if you want to call it that. It is really price control from the top.
Not so long ago we had a report presented in this house showing that the farm implement manufacturers had agreed among themselves upon a system of prices by which they would charge the same price for similar implements. We have had the same situa-

tion in connection with oil, fertilizers and a host of other articles. There is price control by these corporations in their own interests. They know what is best for themselves and it is most unfortunate that the masses of the people in this country can be taken in by the propaganda that is put out and led to believe that fighting each other, struggling against each other, the farmer being set against the labourer, the labour union being set against the professional man, everybody fighting each other, that that is the best system. If that is the best they can offer to humanity, then humanity is in bad shape indeed.
If there is to be a long-range solution of our prices problem it will be necessary to realize that the people of this country should own as much as possible of the means of production, distribution and processing of many commodities. Whether it be through public ownership or the formation of co-opera-lives would not make much difference because it amounts to the same thing in the end. I say in all sincerity that it is necessary for the people to go into public or co-operative ownership of a large sector of the heavy industry of this country. For example, there are the meat packing plants, the farm implement manufacturing and so on. The people should own the means of production and distribution so that the prices charged would be based upon the cost of producing the goods or rendering the service.
Those who know anything about consumer co-operatives realize that at the present time there is no incentive for a co-operative to raise prices. If they do raise prices it is done because it is their policy to have the same price levels as private industry, and then they turn back whatever is over to their members in the form of dividends. They are doing that to save the necks of their good friends the private enterprisers. But in private industry the incentive is to make, as much profit as possible. I am not saying that that is immoral or that that is such a terrible thing. If you are in the water you try to swim and if you operate under this economic system you try to make it work.
One of two things happens. Either you have a deadlock under which all competing forces batter at each other to the point where nobody can win out; you have an epidemic of strikes; you have complete chaos, or you have price dislocation because each sector of the producing and distributing economy is trying to gain its owm advantage.
I am sure that we in Canada have reached the point where we can concentrate on the finer things of life. Surely we have a country

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this resolution, but I do so in the same spirit which has been expressed by several previous speakers. I realize that the resolution will have effect for only a short time, but I believe that its principles will have to be continued in legislation for some time to come. Therefore, in my opinion, it is unnecessary at this stage to debate the principles or the philosophy of controls. I think everyone knows where each individual in this house stands on the question, but I wish to make a few brief remarks in order to indicate the views of what I am certain is the majority of the people I have the honour to represent.
I am quite sure that those who have advocated the' retention of controls and the reimposition of other controls represent the people of this country far more truly than do the Progressive Conservatives in their approach to this question. In my opinion the Progressive Conservative attitude is such that I can readily understand and realize why they are being considered more and more by the people of this country, as the maiden aunts of our political life. I am quite certain that if other constituencies in Canada have the same view as the people I represent, a great majority of the Canadian people are ready to support the principle of controls, the reimposition of certain controls and the re-introduction of certain subsidies. I have no doubt that the people whom I represent are in favour of these things being done by this government.
The majority of the people I represent think the government acted too hastily in a world of uncertainty by removing the controls it has. The people I represent believe that the government should have waited and kept the machinery of controls in operation. I think, Mr. Speaker, it is safe to say that on this question the government is wistfully looking backward in directing our economy, although not so far backward as the Progressive Conservatives.
So far as my constituency is concerned, and I think this is true of the whole country, the
results of the decontrol policy to date have been great increases in food prices in the district and a great increase in the cost of building supplies so necessary to build the many houses that are required at the present time. Cement has greatly increased in price, *as well as nails and lumber products. Just before I came to the house, one of my constituents came to me and gave me certain information with regard to the price of shingles. In the southern interior of British Columbia when war broke out shingles sold, on the average, at about $4 a thousand. Before control was taken off, they were selling at $8 a thousand in my constituency generally. Three days after the control was taken off, one dealer was offering them at S16 a thousand.

That dealer knew that, with winter approaching, there were people who were forced to buy a limited quantity of shingles to complete their building program and he took advantage of his fellow citizens and exercised free enterprise. I could go on at great length giving figures as to increases in costs, but I do not think it is necessary because excellent information in this respect has already been placed on record in this debate.
Support for the principle of controls and the reimposition of controls is widespread. During the recess I had an opportunity to talk to trade unions, co-operative organizations, farmers' organizations, consumers' organizations, women's organizations and various other bodies, and I can say without question that the whole of organized labour in my constituency supports the program of controls. I have in my hand a telegram just received today. It was sent to the Prime Minister, and reads:
_ The following telegram was sent to Prime Minister. Local 480 Mine, Mill and Smelter, representing 3,500 workers urge your government to reimpose price control legislation at present session in accordance with resolution passed at 1947 convention of C.C.L.
That is from the representatives of 3,500 workers in the city of Trail. During the last week since I returned to Ottawa I have received at least a thousand communications from branches of the legion and from veterans and veterans' dependents and a wide crosssection of my constituency urging that an increase be granted in the rate of disability pensions, widows' pensions and the war veterans' allowance. Why? Prior to June, 1946, the classes of people on whose behalf these petitions are being presented were reasonably satisfied. The demand for these increases has, without question, been caused
Transitional Measures Act

by the price increases since June, 1946. That is reflected in the action of the Canadian Legion in British Columbia, which at its last provincial convention passed a strong resolution urging the reimposition of price control. So far as my constituency is concerned, every legion branch in the whole riding supports that program.
I have had an opportunity to talk to farmers' organizations and, without question, all our farmers' organizations, because of their experience since decontrol, are urging the re-imposition of certain controls and subsidies.
I particularly want to mention the plight of the poultry farmer. We have quite an extensive poultry industry in my constituency. In the last month or six weeks, because of the increase in feed prices, thousands of poultry in my riding have been slaughtered. I was talking with a poultry producer who up to this year had been raising, for a number of years, some 3,000 chicks annually. He is going out of business completely. He simply cannot produce eggs that will give him any decent living with prices of feed what they are today. That is going on all over my constituency. Thousands of poultry are being slaughtered because of the increase in the price of feed, and for that reason only.
We have a limited production of hogs and beef cattle. There again, large numbers of people are disposing of their hogs as rapidly as possible, not fattening them to the required weight because of the increase in feed costs, ' and beef cattle sold without finishing on grain.
I have had an opportunity to speak to a number of women's organizations. If you want to realize what the people are thinking you want to listen to what the women's organizations are saying because they are largely representative of the housewives who are faced with the daily problem, with the reality of providing the living for the family. Throughout my whole district, so far as I know, the women's organizations, women's institutes and organizations of that type are supporting the policy that is being advocated from this side of the house. That is true also of a large group of consumer organizations. I judge that this is a very general condition throughout Canada. From the evidence I think it is quite safe to say that the majority of the people of this country want the re-imposition of certain controls and certain subsidies.
Representing the views of a great majority of my constituents I urge the re-imposition of price control on the basic necessities of life, the continuation of rent control and subsidies on milk, butter, bread, feed grains, cotton and wool. In addition, I would ask

the government to keep its promise of January 31, 1946. In that connection I am going to quote from the Ottawa Evening Journal of January 31, 1946. It says:
If costs climb out of line with the general fabric of the price structure both Mr. Ilsley and prices board chairman Donald Gordon promised that the ceilings again would be imposed.
In a letter to hundreds of Canadian manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers, Mr. Gordon emphasized that the ceilings were being suspended, not cancelled.
Mr. Ilsley added the admonition that any abuse of this new price freedom would result in re-imposition of the ceilings.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that all of us will agree that there has been a wide-scale abuse of the new price freedom, and I ask the government to keep its promise according to the Ottawa Evening Journal of January 31, 1946, and re-impose necessary controls.
Mr. G. II. CASTLEDEN (Yorkton): Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us calls for a continuation of the transitional powers act from December 31 of this year to March 31 of next year.
We in this group believe that that period is far too short to be of any value. We feel that with the situation in Canada as it is today and as it is developing, this power wall have to be extended for at least one year and probably longer. This act is the very basis upon which the government has operated its control policy of prices and supplies in Canada for a number of years, and it is quite evident that it must be continued if Canada is to avoid a period of inflation.
I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) in his seat. We can remember the fight he put up over a number of years while the war was on, to hold these controls and keep prices in check and, if necessary, to ration supplies so that they would be distributed fairly and Canada avoid inflation. Since he has left his post as Minister of Finance-whether he left it voluntarily or not I do not know-the government's policy has been what they call orderly decontrol. It seems to me that it has recently developed into a disorderly rout because of the rate at which the government is taking off subsidies, throwing controls out the window and letting the Winnipeg grain exchange and other bodies take control of prices in this country. Canada is heading very rapidly into a period of inflation which has all the people in every part of Canada alarmed and apprehensive about the future. I think there is plenty of evidence to show that if these controls are discontinued in Canada we shall face a period of inflation similar to what happened in the United States. This

Transitional Measures Act
government cannot claim that they did not know what would happen. They had the experience of what happened in the United States when OPA was discontinued at the end of June, 1946, and the spiral of inflation and high prices there which finally brought action from the United States government.
Our criticism of the government is that they have failed to use these powers sufficiently to stop the inflationary trend in the rise of prices. We believe that, so long as production and trade are below normal, it will be necessary to have these controls and these powers in the hands of the government, whatever government is in power. We do not like to see them giving in to the requests of the official opposition in this house to take these controls off and try to let the whole thing level itself off. They maintain that if you just let these things go, they will adjust themselves. They will not adjust themselves in this period of scarcity. They will not adjust themselves until production is at its proper level, until there are sufficient supplies to go around and until normal trade is returned to the world.
I wish to deal particularly with one act of the government, namely, its decontrol policy on coarse grain, which has been referred to nere previously this evening and its particular affect, not only upon the coarse grain producers ,n the west, but upon the whole Canadian economy. I want to point out, if I can, .vhere we think a serious mistake was made and try to find out, if we can, some justification for the government doing what they did. [f the Canadian people and parliament can be shown that what the government did is justifiable, that there was some reason behind it which made it necessary, I think the Canadian people will accept the government's reasons if they are right and just.
About October 20 the cabinet announced its decision to discontinue the subsidies on coarse grain and to discontinue coarse grain price control. From that date on, the grain exchange in Winnipeg would be the deciding factor with regard to the price of coarse grain. The government cannot plead that they did not know what the effects would be. The farmers who were fortunate enough to have a coarse grain crop in the west have been placed in a precarious position. First of all, when the crop was ripe and ready for the market they were stiill under controlled prices in the west, with sixty-seven cents for barley. They did not know what to do. They did not know whether they should hang on to it or sell it. Would the government, after they had sold it, release tire controls and let the price go up
and the farmer take the loss? Or should they hang on to it? It is interesting to notice that when the grain became available for the market, regulations went out to take all quotas off the delivery of coarse grains, apparently as an incentive to the western farmer to deliver his coarse grain at the old controlled price of sixty-seven cents. However, when the Minister of Agriculture came back from England, he made an announcement to the effect that it was not. the intention of the government to alter their coarse grain policy this year. Last year-I believe about March of 1947-under price control the government permitted an increase of about ten cents in the price of coarse grain. All the farmers who had delivered coarse grain from their 1946 crop prior to that time were then paid an equalization fee. The ten cents was paid out to them, and the farmers had no reason to suspect that the same would not be done this year.

I do not know how the government intends to do it. I do not see how the government can justify its action of taking coarse grains price controls
