off, letting the grain exchange make that money and then tax the Canadian people to make it up, if the government intends to do that. The minister will probably make a statement as to what he intends to do.
The farmers who now find the price of barley up to SI.28 are wondering what they are going to do about their crops next year. Shall they sow their farms to coarse grain, or shall they sow them to wheat? The relationship between the grains is so much out of line at the present time that they do not know what to do. There is still uncertainty as to what might happen to coarse grain prices next year. As lion, members can see, the farmer is in an unfortunate position. When the farmer of this country goes out to buy anything, whether it is oils, binder twine, grease, farm machinery or anything else he requires, he has to go and ask the other chap how much it costs; because he is the buyer and the other fellow is the seller, he has to pay what the other fellow says. But when he goes to sell anything there has never been a time, except under price control, that anybody ever told him anything but what price he was going to get for his goods; and lie sometimes had to take a very low price. As the farmer says, "Every time I go to buy anything, they keep squeezing the price up. And when I go to sell anything they keep squeezing the price down, and I am squeezed out." Price control, at any rate prevented the squeezing of prices down in spite of the fact there is nothing to prevent the squeezing of prices up.
All the farmer is asking is that the relationship between his cost of production and his selling price be such that he will not be squeezed out. The labourer is in exactly the same position. The labourer has to go out and buy the goods that are required to maintain his family, such as food, clothing and shelter, and he is told what prices he shall pay for them. When he goes to sell the only thing he has to sell, which is the sweat of his brow, somebody is telling him what price he shall get for it. They squeeze the one up and the other down, and he is being squeezed out. All he is asking for is that there be a proper relation between the cost of the things which go to make up his cost of living and the value that he can get for the sweat of his brow, so that he will not be squeezed out. I believe the labourer would be quite willing to agree to the control of labour and the control of wages so long as that proper relationship was left there, so that he would not be squeezed out or could not be squeezed out, in spite of what the hon. member for

Peel (Mr. Graydon) said the other day about our not stating any such policy and using the word "hypocrisy," under protection.
I am thinking of a farmer in my own constituency-a young man starting out on his farm, a veteran of the war-with 3,000 bushels of barley. He did not know what to do. About the first week in October he sold 3,000 bushels of barley. By the end of the month, instead of getting 67 cents, he would have got $1.27, and he is out $1,800. which would have been a substantial payment on his farm. He does not take very kindly to this sort of thing. Then the farmer who feeds-and there are a great many who do-cannot feed hogs with barley at $1.28 and sell those hogs at the prices that prevail today. An unfortunate thing has happened. Along with the minister's statement there was nothing to let the farmer know that relative prices of hogs would be maintained and the result has been the destruction of hogs on a scale that should not have taken place in view of the shortage of food throughout the world at the present time. The fact is that farmers have been selling hogs underweight and killing them off.
The cattle feeders are in the same predicament. The cost of coarse grain feeds to cattle farmers is such that many farmers in eastern Canada are up in arms. They cannot obtain coarse grain feeds at the prices they paid under price control and make a living out of the business, and with the cost of feeds at the figure it has reached today their business is practically wiped out.
The poultry producers are in the same position. A previous speaker has told us what the poultry raisers are doing in his part of the country. They are simply killing off their poultry because it does not pay them to operate.
What will be the result of all this? The result will be a further shortage of food and, with that shortage, higher and higher prices all along the line. We on this side of the house cannot see what justification there is for the government's action. They must be thinking of the consumer, but the consumer is bound to face higher prices and a rising cost of living. The milk producer cannot feed dairy cattle and pay present prices demanded for feeds. He is already getting so much per quart for his milk; but if feeds go up in price, the cost of milk will go up because he cannot take a loss, and therefore the milk producers are asking for higher prices. Butter prices are going to go up and, as I say, the cost of living is rising all along the line.

Transitional Measures Act
The consumers do not liKe this rising cost of living. Indeed, the rise in the cost of living is one of the most rapid trends in inflation that Canada has faced. Well, if it is not the Canadian producer or the Canadian consumer who is getting the benefit, who is it? Surely the amount paid in subsidies, as far as the taxpayer is concerned, does not justify the lifting of the controls. Whoj then, stands to benefit by the action of the government? There is only one group I know of; that is the group that evidently has been pounding away for months and months for the removal of price controls and subsidy on coarse grains, and they want it off wheat. They are the manipulators and speculators on the Winnipeg grain exchange. Apparently they are the ones who are making the millions. As far as I can see, they are the only ones who are making money and the Canadian people are being forced to pay.
The cost of living is going up; you have inflation, and what does the government intend to do to put a stop to it? We shall certainly vote for the extension of these controls, and what the government do to them will be the result of their own policy. They certainly know what the opposition members in this party want, and they know what many of their own members want; that is, the reimposition of controls. They want to see the wartime prices and trade board re-established so far as the essentials of life are concerned, so that proper price control will be maintained to stop the spiral of inflation. The Canadian people will be willing to see subsidies continue so long as it prevents the cost of living from going up and up, as it is doing today. If the Winnipeg grain exchange alone stands to gain, then I think the Canadian people would like to see it closed, and I join with those who have expressed that opinion.
I do not know what the government intend to do in this matter. Perhaps they think there has been too much taxation, and perhaps the Minister of Finance will speak later on and give us his view. But the Canadian taxpayers are looking at the result of the 1947 budget, one of the important clauses of which provided that the Excess Profits Tax Act should be discontinued as of December 31 of this year. Apparently excess profits will be allowed to go untaxed then. '
The government will follow whatever policy it intends for its own good or for the good of the Canadian people; but the people are watching carefully, and if the government does not exercise controls properly so as to stop inflation, it will have to answer, because it is evident that the rate at which we are travelling at the present time is leading us to
inflation and chaos. The government, I say, will be held responsible for what happens.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Some of the statements made in this debate ought to be answered at this time. These statements have to do largely with that part of the removal of price controls which was concerned with feed grain. Many statements have been made with regard to it which are not in accordance with the facts as they have been presented from time to time both before and since the removal of the ceilings on coarse grains, and I think it would be unfair, both to members of this house and to the country at large, to leave those statements unanswered.
The fact is that we have had control on feed grains for some considerable time. That control was put on at a time when the price of grain was quite low, back in 1941. The government decided at that time not to put the same kind of control on wheat as had been placed on coarse grains. In other words, wheat was allowed to increase in price from time to time at a rate which was quite considerable as compared with any increases which were permitted in connection with coarse grains.
The reason for that was obvious at the time. The government was attempting to keep down the cost of living; and in an effort to do so, under the system which is being advocated at this time particularly by those who belong to the C.C.F. party in the house, the government established ceiling prices on food. Of course, foods that were produced through the feeding of oats and barley were regulated among others. Not only had the foods themselves to be regulated", but price of the grains that entered into their production had to be regulated, and so we put a ceiling on coarse grains. That ceiling was obviously a low one. It was not very long before the farmers who were producers of feed grain raised objection and properly so. When they did raise objection to the ceilings being held at the levels at which they were first established, the government adjusted the prices upwards, or adjusted the returns upwards, by agreeing to issue permits to sell some of the oats and barley in the United States at higher prices and to permit participation by the farmers in regard to those oats and barley.
This resulted in very little in the way of participation. The amount of grain sold was not as great as had been expected and the price received was not as high as had been anticipated. So at that time the government guaranteed the farmers for the next year an additional ten cents a bushel on oats and
Transitional Measures Act

fifteen cents a bushel on barley. In other words, when the grain was delivered we took out of the treasury of Canada what could have amounted to a subsidy of ten cents on oats and what could have amounted to a subsidy of fifteen cents on barley and paid it to the farmers. A record was kept, and if the government-or the people of Canada, if you like to put it in that way-took a loss on that grain that loss was chalked up to that particular year's experience. If any profit was made by selling that grain in the United States, that profit was passed on- to the farmers by means of participation. In some years, just speaking from memory, I believe that participation amounted to as much as five cents a bushel on barley and a lesser amount on oats over and above the fifteen and ten cents, but in any event the effort was made to increase the return to the producer of oats and barley, and at all times the effort was made to keep oats and barley in proper relationship as far as return was concerned with the return being obtained from wheat. The idea, of course, was that if you allowed wheat to get out of line with oats and barley, that is out of line upwards, you would get more wheat than you desired or, to put it in another way, you would get less feed grain than was necessary to feed the livestock we had on our farms. We followed that policy right through the war.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: Would the minister say how many years that subsidy was given?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: I believe it started in 1942 and continued until last year.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext: Just to complete the picture, prior to that you had endeavoured to encourage the increased production of coarse grains by other methods as well?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Yes, one year before; but I will come to that later on in connection with something else. In 1946 there was a great deal of complaint as to the manner in which coarse grains were being handled. I do not think a' considerable portion of that complaint was soundly based; nevertheless it was made. The farmers both east and west were dissatisfied with what was taking place in relation to coarse grains. On March 17 last it was announced in this house that the policy which had been followed up to that time would be dropped and provision was made to reimburse those who had sold their barley early, while provision was made otherwise, through the amount of oats that had been sold in the United States, to take care of the claims of those who had sold oats in the period from August 1 down to March 17.

While that provision was made, the policy which had been followed up to that time was reversed; instead of the producers of coarse grains being paid any amount, either because of sales in the United States or for any other reason, a drawback to the eastern farmer or, to put it in other terms, a subsidy was paid on grain that was purchased and fed on farms east of Fort William. When that announcement was made in the house on March 17, with the policy to come into effect the next day, there was considerable discussion on the floor of the house and also throughout the country as to whether the control [DOT] of prices was to continue beyond August 1, 1947. During last session provision was only made for continuing these drawbacks until August 1, and everyone surmised from this that the controls would probably be taken off on August 1. A few moments ago the hon. member for York-ton (Mr. Castleden) suggested that because no one said anything definite about the matter the farmer had a right to expect that the controls were not going to be taken off at all.
I submit to the house, Mr. Speaker, that it would have been absolutely impossible, in fairness to all the farmers of Canada, for anyone to have made an announcement in advance as to what would be done in regard . to that particular matter.
The reason for saying that is obvious. If we had said the controls would be taken off on August 1, naturally a very considerable amount of grain would not have been delivered at all, or certainly if it had been delivered it would have been held along the way by some person and would not have found its way to the feeders in different parts of Canada. It was only the uncertainty as to whether or not prices would be changed on August 1 that caused the grain to be delivered, together with-the fact that throughout the whole period of control, both before and after the act, farmers had been treated in a way which' those who might desire to do so could justify as being reasonable. So the farmers went on delivering grain. Then, when we reached August 1, it was definitely stated by farm organizations, by farmers, and by those who came to Ottawa to make representations, that it would be a mistake, to remove controls from feed grain until controls were taken off all the products that are produced by feeding grain. Already we had removed the controls from most dairy products, but they were still on meat; and it was suggested that the controls on meat and grain should be taken off at |he same time.
An intimation was given to the people of Canada at that time that, in addition to what had been voted during last session, sufficient

Transitional Measures Act
funds would be provided to take care of any drawbacks for a two months' period; and the statement was also made at that time that the controls ought to be taken off at the same time. The most anyone can say is that the farmers had a right to expect that those controls would be taken off during that period of two months, which brought us down to October
1.	So any real complaint there may be with regard to that situation applies to the period from October 1 to October 21, a period of three weeks. I do not think it is any secret anywhere in Canada, or anything misunderstood by anyone in the country as to why controls were not taken off during these three weeks. About the middle of September there was a packers' strike in Canada and, whether the judgment of the government was good or bad in the matter, it was not considered a fair thing or an action which would be likely to bring the best results to all the people of Canada-producers and consumers alike-to take that action while the strike was on.
There have been some suggestions during the debate in the house, that the decision had something to do with a certain election in Canada. It just so happened that the election date and the date the strike ended were almost the same, and the controls were taken off the last day of the strike, or the day it was announced that the strike was over; nevertheless that was the judgment, and that was the reason, and the only one, why the controls had not been taken off at an earlier day.
The only criticism made in' the debate on that point is that some farmers sold their coarse grains during that period, and sold them at a lower price than they could have obtained after October 21. Some suggestion has been made that the government ought to do something about the matter. As was stated a few minutes ago by one hon. member, I was in Saskatchewan at the time the controls were taken off and addressed half a dozen very large meetings in farming areas in the five or six days following the taking off of those controls. At each of those meetings a number of men asked the question as to what might be done in respect of grain that had been delivered prior to October 21. and more particularly grain delivered after October 1. Some of them said they thought they were justified in going back to September 15, feeling that, in the light of all that had being said prior to that, there might be some justification for saying'that they might have expected controls to be taken off on September 15, and that anything done prior to that date they had done with their eyes open. It was pointed out, however, that anything after that date was done more or less
under pressure by the government and by farmers elsewhere in Canada to have grain delivered, because that grain was required in order to feed livestock elsewhere.
Whatever the feeling might be, the facts are these, that from the time the crop was harvested in western Canada down to October 21, more feed was delivered by the farmers to the elevators than was delivered in the same period of the preceding year. I state that in order to deny the suggestion made to the effect that farmers in western Canada had anything whatsoever to do with keeping grain away from farmers in eastern Canada. The . farmers in western Canada delivered their grain in as great quantities as they had in the preceding year.
There was one other suggestion which was made in the last speech and which I do not think was justified. I do not think it is necessary to be either for or against the grain exchange in order to state the facts. The facts are that about half of this grain was taken in by the pool elevator companies, particularly in Saskatchewan. The other half was taken in by the line elevator companies.
I have made as close inquiry as it is possible to make with regard to the matter, and I am informed that the proportion of the grain which was delivered to both the line elevators and the pool elevators which was sold is almost exactly the same; and that the proportion which was sold, too, bears a reasonable relationship to the proportion sold in other years down to the same time.
In other words, neither the pool elevators nor the line elevators held grain off the market in order to make others pay more for it after October 21. They both took delivery of grain from the farmers and they paid the farmers for it according to the payments provided for. Then they sold the grain to those who were expected to deliver it to farmers elsewhere in Canada in order that it be fed, I think that much ought to be said for both the line elevator companies and the pool elevator companies.	.

speechtext:
What is the exact
amount handled in each case?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
I should not like to attempt to give that information because, in the first place, I have not the exact figures here, although I know just about what they were. But in the second place, this matter is under consideration by the different companies, and any information which has been given to me with regard to either the pools or the other companies individually I do not think I should place before the public at the present time, when they are dealing with those matters.
Transitional Measures Act

But what I found was this, that a certain number of bushels-about half-were delivered to the pool elevator companies, particularly in Saskatchewan, and that about the same proportion of the grain delivered to one or the other was sold. That grain moved out at the lower, not at the higher price. But it got into the hands of those who sold feeds in eastern Canada, and some things are alleged to have happened. At one place one thing happened, and at another place a different thing. I am not going to attempt at the present time to lay blame on those who handled the grain for not having allowed it to get into the farmers' hands at a lower price, but to have held it . until a higher price could be obtained for it. But I am informed, on the best information I can get, that it was not the farmers of western Canada, that it was not the pool elevator companies and that it was not the line elevator companies that held this grain off the market.
Having said that, may I add this, that at those meetings where questions were asked statements were made. I could tell a story very similar to the one told by the hon. member for Yorkton and which might be applied to my own district, where a young returned man sold grain the day before the announcement was made, and the next morning rushed to the elevator to find whether they had sold it or not, only to learn that they had already sold it to a milling company in the vicinity. The milling company was already turning it into feed to be sold to the farmers in the surrounding district. So there was nothing he could do about it; it just happened that fast. There were many cases of that kind, and of other kinds, where people felt that they had legitimate claims upon someone.
I said this to them; and I repeat it here, because I think it is something which should go out to the country. I said, "Half the grain has been delivered to the pool elevators". And I have since found out that that is about correct. Half the grain is usually delivered to the line elevator companies and half to the pool elevator companies. I went on to say, "If I know the poo! elevator people I am quite certain that they, themselves, will deal with that question so far as it is possible for them to deal with it," When they asked the question, "Well, what do you think they might do?" at that time I did not have the correct figures; but I said. "Let us assume that so much grain has been delivered to the elevator company and that only 20 per cent of it has been sold"; I can say now that a much larger percentage of it was sold; I went on to say,
"I think what the pooling organization would do would be to set aside grain which was -bought before October 21 and sell it separ-

ately from other grain taken in during this year and pay the money obtained therefrom into a pool. Then, from that pool they would treat all persons alike who had delivered into it,"
I said, "I do not know just what the procedure would be but I assume that that is what they would do. I would assume that if they do that, then the other companies will do a similar thing, or the other companies may do it whether the pools do it or not because they might consider it to be good business. But I would think that would be what would be done by those who have taken delivery of the grain. I have more reason now to think that is what they will do than I had then for thinking that was what they would do, but I thought it was the reasonable thing to be done." Then I went on to say that it would be absolutely impossible for the government to say at that stage what they would do in connection with the matter. Any statement they would make in connection with the matter could be used by those concerned either to make money for themselves or to lose money for someone else. Therefore the only position to take was that these organizations would in due course be in a position to announce what they were going to do and to make representations to the government as to what they thought the government ought to do.
No later than today I found, by making inquiries, that there are still elevator companies which have not yet sold all the grain taken in prior to October 21. Until those sales are cleared up, it will be impossible for the companies to deal with the matter in an intelligent way and, until they make their representations, it certainly will be impossible lor the government to give further consideration to the matter.
The other question raised was in connection with the buying of grain on the open market. I am not going to discuss tonight whether trading in oats and barley should remain on the open market, or whether they should be placed under the control of the wheat board; that is not a matter under discussion at the moment. The fact is that on October 21 and down to the present the government has had no authority to place oats and barley under the control of the wheat board. If price controls were to be taken off on October 21 or at any other time since parliament last prorogued, it would be impossible for the government to have taken that action. Until this house met, it has been impossible to give further consideration to the possibility of doing it.

Transitional Measures Act
I would point out that we have continued our control on wheat by making a contract with Great Britain and by the selling of the wheat not under contract on the markets of the world. We have established the amount that can be paid to farmers in the way of advance, payments on wheat. Up to the present time the advance payment made has been S1.35 a bushel. The government has stated on a number of occasions that authority would be asked, when the house was in session, to pay an advance higher than $1.35. It will be remembered that an amendment was moved at the last session asking that we pay $1.55 as an' advance instead of S1.35. We stated at that time that the question would be discussed when we were sure that there was sufficient money in the pool to make a payment of that kind.
Some little time ago it was announced tlhat sufficient funds were there to make a payment of at least that amount. No announcement has yet been made as to the amount that is to be paid, but it is pretty generally understood that it will be at least $1.55. Therefore every farmer who has been looking at the question is entitled to believe that he will receive $1.55 a bushel for wheat over the five year period. When he comes to that conclusion he also comes to a conclusion as to what the value of barley and oats will be. The value of feed barley, not malting barley, based upon $1.55 wheat is between $1.15 and $1.25 as conditions have been varying. The value of oats is somewhere between eighty and ninety cents a bushel.
Controls were taken off on October 21 and because of the situation existing, if for no other reason, oats and barley are dealt with on the open market. An examination of the records will show that the ceiling on barley throughout that period has been around $1.25 a bushel, with the floor being around $1.12 or $1.14 a bushel. The price has finally settled at about $1.25. The ceiling on oats has been close to ninety cents, with the floor being around eight-two or eighty-three cents. In other words, with the market operating as it is, the price of feed grains to farmers in eastern Canada and in other parts of Canada has borne about the same relationship to wheat as the government would have been compelled to place upon oats and barley if they had followed the suggestion of ihe organized farmers that we do not take off the controls but raise the ceiling to a level comparable with wheat and put these grains under the wheat board. In other words, the results would have been almost identical.
I repeat that I am not arguing the question as to what should have been done under all the circumstances; I simply am pointing out that 'the fact remains that controls are not off feed grains. The statement has been made over and over again that price controls have been taken off feed grains. The most effective price control is not off feed grains; the most effective control on feed grains is the fact that there is an established value for wheat. Then, in addition, entry into the United States is prevented. Feed grains cannot be exported from this country; they must all be delivered to the farmers of Canada for feed.
If the price of barley goes any higher during any period of time than $1.25 a bushel, farmers all over this country will feed wheat instead of barley. Whenever they start to do that, the price of barley will come down a little. We have had an application to permit the shipment of a whole boatload of barley to the United States because of a lack of buyers for the grain. We said, "No, the boundary is to be kept closed". When you take those two matters together they form just as effective a control upon feed grains and upon the ceiling on feed grains as there has been at any time.
And meat.

My hon. friend saj-s, "and meat." That brings me to another statement which has been made in reference to this same question on a number of occasions, namely, that the price of meat in the British contract is the ceiling price. The price of meat in the British contract is not. the ceiling price and never has been. The price of meat is the floor price. If one examines the records which I have of the deliveries of meat he will find that we have not been able to secure sufficient meat, offering the floor price for it every day on every market in Canada. At every packing plant in Canada, at every place where we can pick up meat, there has been a floor price, which is the price in the meat contract, offered for that meat, and we have not been able to obtain sufficient meat because someone else is paying more for it. In other words, the price in the contract is not tihe ceiling but the floor price.
How much have you had to pay above the contract price?
We have not paid anything over the contract price.
How much under?

We have not bought below. We have offered the price in the British contract for both bacon and beef, and we
Transitional Measures Act

have not been able to get beef at those prices to the amount of more than 36,000,000 pounds, when we contracted to deliver 120,000,000 pounds. My hon. friend, if' he knows the business of the ranchers he presumes to represent, will know that the reason we did not get more beef was that somebody else did pay more. It does not matter whether it was only a cent more; somebody paid more and got the beef. In other words, the contract price is not the ceiling price; it is the floor price.
It is essentially that.
Why did you not buy the beef on the hoof to protect the farmer?

That is another question that my hon. friend and I can argue at some other stage of the session. But the facts are as I have stated them. The prices in the British contracts are the floor prices and not the ceiling.
No answer, eh?

I would be out of order in answering. I am trying to keep myself in order. We can discuss that question at another time.
A further consideration is that the price is under control through the fact that we have controls still on the boundary line. It is under control, too, through the fact that the product is associated with wheat, and it is under further control through the fact that we have an embargo against the shipment of meat or any other farm products, with few exceptions, to the United States. All these things have helped us to keep a decided control upon these particular products down to the present time; and to be stating, as my hon. friends do over and over again in this house, that the controls are off, is stating what is not a fact in relation to these particular products. The most effective kind of control that you can have is the permit system, under which we are not issuing permits for commodities to be sold in the United States, plus the fact that we have contracts with Brit-these commodities can be taken off this market and sent to Britain, and if we take sufficient of these commodities off the market here to place the quantity below demand, the price to the consumer in Canada tends to go up. When there is sufficient left here to satisfy the demand, the price tends to go down.
What I should like to say to my hon. friends opposite is this. You cannot have this thing both ways. One cannot be arguing that the cost of living should not go up as a result of what 'has happened to food prices,

and at the same time argue that the farmer ought to get more. The two things just do not go together. If the farmer is to get more for the products that he has to sell, then the consumer somewhere has to pay more for the food products he consumes. When these two things are considered I would say that it is not sound to be arguing both ways at the same time. We must have either one thing or the other.	.
We feel that the general experience of farmers is that they have not done too badly over the last four or five years at least. When I make that statement I am not trying to say that the farmers are doing as well as they ought to do, because I quite realize, as every member of the house realizes, that there is no one who experiences greater difficulty in getting all that is coming to him than a group of farmers operating as they do in Canada on 750,000 individual farms all across this country. It is difficult for them to get all that is coming to them, and I do not believe that they have ever had all that is coming to them.
Nevertheless, having said that, I should like to point out that both the net income and the gross income of farmers in Canada in the last four years has been almost double what it was in the previous four years, and in those four years it was a little better than it had ever been before except at the end of the first war. When that is true, the situation is not just as bad as it has been painted on the other side of the house. When one can say, too, that the farmers' estimated gross income for this year is just a little more than double what it was in the best year we ever had prior to 1942, again one can see that the situation has not been quite so bad as it has been painted.
I think I heard a whisper over there about the income tax. It has not changed since last year, but I am not going to discuss the income tax because it does not affect the picture very much so far as the farmers across Canada are concerned. That, again, is another indication that the farmer finds it most difficult to get the income to which he is entitled. But having said that, let me repeat that the farmer has been doing better during the last few years than he ever did at any previous time, and I think that is the reason why my hon. friends of the C.C.F. have been arguing so strongly that we ought to continue to do the same thing in the future as we have been doing during these years. They have repeated over and over again that prices have been stabilized and the farmer has done well.

Look at what he has to buy-

My hon. friend says, "Look at what he has to buy". I understand that in his district the farmers for the first time have had to buy feed. So now they are beginning to realize that some other people do run out of feed sometimes. At every session of this house down to the present the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has been saying there is no feed shortage in Canada.
That brings me back to a question which was asked a few moments ago by the hon. member for Humboldt. What is the position in relation to feed in Canada? Back at the beginning of the war we did start to encourage the farmers to take land out of wheat, as was suggested. We paid them $4 an acre to take land out of wheat, and they reduced their acreage from between 28,000,000 and
29,000,000 acres down to between 17,000,000 and 18,000,000 acres. That was done for the purpose of doing what we were asked to do by the British people earlier in the war. They were switching over 6,000,000 acres of their land from the production of livestock to the production of cereals, and they suggested that we turn over some of our land from the production of cereals to the production of livestock and ship them the products as we were able to do so. We followed that practice down until 1944 and 1945. By then there had started all across the world an agitation to get more cereals to feed people at the end of the war.
I should like to remind the members of this house of another thing that happened at that time. It seems to have been entirely forgotten-

I am sorry to interrupt
the hon. gentleman, but he has exhausted his time.
Go ahead.
Continue.

With the consent of the
house.

It seems to have been
entirely forgotten that a certain gentleman came to Canada from Great Britain and spoke in farm meetings right across this country. I listened to him speak to the wheat pool at their annual meeting in the city of Regina. In that meeting he made the bold statement that, after the war was over, Britain was going to again trade bicycles for bacon to Denmark. After considering the representations that were made in favour of cereals and after considering what that kind of statement meant, not only the government but the farmers began to shift back.
On the advice of the government.

Yes, with the advice
of the government. Up until last year they had put back into wheat 8,000,000 acres of the 10,000.000, and they were utilizing the other 2,000,000 acres in addition to what they had in coarse grains before for the production of feed grains. That was all done, as has been stated, under suggestion, or rather the first part of it was done on more than suggestion, namely, as a result of paying so much an acre to get it done; and the second part of it was accomplished by suggesting that people throughout the world are going to require more wheat.
It will be recalled that in this house ne one did more in that direction than the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken). In this house just two years ago every member of the official opposition was taking the position that we should go even farther in that direction, and that we should put another
3,000,000 acres of land into wheat. True and all as it is that the production of livestock and the production of dairy products have gone down, they would have gone down a great deal more if the farmers had done that.
I am not going to argue the question of whether it should have gone down more. I am going to say this. There are people in the world who still think that we should have put our livestock production down to a lower level than it is now, and that we should be selling cereals in greater quantity than we are doing now. The government was not in agreement with those who took that position. But the official opposition took that position two years ago. If they were right then, there is not any logic whatsoever in their arguing no\s that we ought to have more livestock products in Canada; because we are feeding all the feed grain that we are growing in Canada, and we have had to put an embargo on at the United States boundary line in order to keep enough here to feed what we shall have left after all these little pigs and chickens are slaughtered. We are only going to have enough, after the stock has been further reduced in Canada, to complete the feeding of the livestock we have here. I can understand an argument to the effect that we ought to be producing more cereals in order to help the people who are threatened with starvation somewhere or who may be threatened with it.

I want to ask a question of the minister, Mr. Speaker. Am
Transitional Measures Act

I right in saying that we were led to believe last session that there would be as much this year?
You were right in thinking we were trying to get as much.
Am I right in saying that the minister told us in this house that there would be as much wheat coming from the west this year as last year?

No. The bon. member is not right in saying that. He is right in saying that the farmers both here' and in the west attempted to do what we asked 'them to do last year. Last year we asked the farmers in the eastern part of Canada to put more land into feed grain. The farmers of eastern Canada laid out their plans to do that, but it mined every day of the seeding season and they were able to put in only sixty per cent of what they had intended to put in. So they just could not grow the other forty per cent. But that is not any fault of the government, and it is not any fault of the farmers. They did everything they could to get that grain. There is the further fact that the western farmer did put 1,200,000 more acres into barley. He lowered his oat acreage somewhat, and that was suggested to him in order to get more barley. But he put that acreage into barley, and then he sat during the last month before harvest and watched his crop disappear because of drought. So he has not as much barley this year in spite of the fact that he did everything he possibly could in order to get it. In other words, the farmers right across this country attempted to do the thing they were asked to do. They did their very best to accomplish it, but they were not able to do so because of the prevailing weather conditions.
Now it has been suggested that the recent conference broke down or that something happened to it, and that suggestion has been made, 'based upon the fact that there is some difficulty in connection with the drawing up of the agreements. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that any discussions that were taking place as between Britain and this government had nothing whatsoever to do with anything that happened in connection with acreages as dealt with at the conference. All the plans and the documents were drawn up; some of them had been submitted to the provinces before any delegation at all was here from the old land. The fact was that what we did say 'to the farmers this year was this. We said, "If you will try again to do what you tried to do last year, that should be

absolutely satisfactory, provided that you are able to accomplish it". So what we have said is, "Go out and sow the same number of acres, if you can. Try again to put in more oats and- barley in the east; try again to put in more 'barley in the west. If you are successful this year, we shall be able to increase our production of livestock next year. But if you are not successful, then, of course, we shall have to carry on very much as we are".
That is the position in relation to feed grains, and I thought it should be placed upon the record tonight in view of the fact that so many other things have been said with regard to that question. I shall leave any discussion with regard to the contracts until the other resolution is before the house.

I rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. During my absence the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) made certain statements in regard to myself which I am asking, through you, that he withdraw and retract. I do so under standing order 41, and I read only the pertinent words:
No member shall . . . use offensive words . . . against either house, or against any member thereof.
I particularly refer you to citation 297, which reads as follows:
The imputation of bad motives, or motives different from those acknowledged, misrepresenting the language of another, or accusing him, in his turn, of misrepresentation, charging him with falsehood or deceit; or contemptuous or insulting language of any kind; all these are unparliamentary and call for prompt interference.
That is, on the part of the Speaker. The words spoken by the hon. gentleman-and again I point out that it was done in my absence; when I came in he immediately went on to some other matter-
Oh, Oh.

There is an implication there, Mr. Speaker, that I am going to ask the hon. member to withdraw. I did not go on immediately to another matter when he entered the house. He was not here when the house opened. He might have known that, as a result of the type of speech he made, there would be a reply to it.
He got what he deserved.

The statement in question was: "Deliberately tried to leave a wrong impression". The other statement is, "did not display the integrity generally shown in this house". These statements, I submit, are not in keeping with the things that we as gentlemen say of one another, and I am asking for a withdrawal.

The hon. member for Lake Centre is using exactly the same method now that he used in his speech. He did not quote the sentence-
I quoted the exact words.

You quoted certain words out of the sentence, just the same as you quoted certain words out of the statement without reading the whole statement. The sentence was:
I thought the speech he delivered did not display the integrity and quality generally shown in this house by the hon. gentleman.
As regards the other statement, that I thought he deliberately tried to misrepresent- is that the word?

Left the wrong
impression.

That he "deliberately
attempted to leave a wrong impression with the house". As far as the word "'deliberately" is concerned, I have already asked that it be deleted from Hansard, but as far as the wrong impression is concerned, I leave it to a reading of Hansard if my statement was not correct.

speechtext: May I suggest, in regard to this incident, that I do not think there is much difference of opinion between the two hon. members. If Your Honour reviews the situation over-night I think the proper corrections will appear to have been made.
I ask for a withdrawal of it.
Such delicacy of feeling!

I understand the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has written down what he has said. Will he be kind enough to send it to me? I understand he has written on a piece of paper what he said, and I should like to see it. The hon. member for Melfort had said:
I thought the speech he delivered did not display the integrity and quality generally shown in this house by the hon. gentleman. I
I would call the attention of the house to the word " integrity," and I would call the attention of the hon. member to standing order 41. citation 297, which reads:

Unfortunately, when the sentences in question were pronounced early tonight, there was so much noise in the chamber that I could not understand them. Knowing very well the hon. member for Melfort, knowing that he is a gentleman, I am sure that he can find a way to amend his sentence without attacking the integrity of the hon. member for Lake Centre and I would ask him to do so.
I would be pleased to do that, Mr. Speaker. I think the action was enough to decide whether there was any integrity involved.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I ask for an absolute withdrawal.
You got it.
Leave it to the house.

Order. Do I understand that the hon. member will withdraw the word "integrity"? I believe that both members have shown to the house that they are gentlemen, and if exception is taken to the word "integrity" in that connection, and a correction is made, I do not see why any member should object.

I have certainly followed with interest the discourse of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and his arguments, and I am sure that many of us sympathize with him and his staff in the difficulties in which they find themselves. The public will be somewhat disappointed that he did not give them a lead from now on, and I am sure the nation is waiting for a statement from him in his official capacity to give it that lead for the coming year.
Before taking up his arguments, I wish to deal with some statements made by the leader of the group to my left and by other hon. members, and I wonder if I might call it eleven o'clock and adjourn the debate.
On motion of Mr. Ross (Souris) the debate was adjourned.
